M82), Na+ was largely confined to the bundle sheath, whereas in salt-tolerant, Na+-including wild relatives, Na+ accumulated throughout the blade mesophyll. Consistent with these cell population-specific Na+ patterns, M82, but not Solanum pennellii, exhibited reduced symplastic transport and plasmodesma permeability under salt stress. A genetic screen combined with transcriptome profiling implicated Plasmodesmata-Located Protein 1 (PDLP1), a regulator of callose-mediated plasmodesma closure, in establishing symplastic domains in M82 that restrict Na+ movement into the mesophyll. Moreover, PDLP1 expression was negatively correlated with mesophyll Na+ levels across wild and domesticated tomatoes. Collectively, these results link cellular Na+ enrichment patterns to symplastic connectivity and suggest that PDLP1-mediated regulation of plasmodesmata contributes to leaf-level salt-tolerance strategies.

works.title: Phenylboronic acid-induced defects in maize roots are independent of rhamnogalacturonan-II dimerization
works.abstract: Soil boron deficiency is a global abiotic stress, negatively impacting on crop yield. In the dicot model species Arabidopsis thaliana, inhibition of root elongation is one of the earliest symptoms of boron deficiency. In the monocot model maize (Zea mays L.), boron deficiency-induced root defects are widely unexplored. In this study, we assessed boron deficiency-induced defects in the primary root system of maize and tested the suitability of phenylboronic acid (PBA) as boron deficiency mimic by performing phenotypic, histological, molecular, and biochemical analyses. Our analyses showed that boron deficiency and PBA resulted in similar defects in primary root elongation and lateral root density. The PBA-induced defects, however, were much stronger than those induced by boron deficiency, particularly regarding lateral root development. We provide evidence that the PBA-induced defects were caused by the boric acid moiety and show that both boron deficiency and PBA altered the levels of auxin and reactive oxygen species. Strikingly, PBA did not affect rhamnogalacturonan-II (RG-II) dimerization. Interference of boron-mediated RG-II crosslinking, however, was previously proposed to be the mode of action of PBA in planta. Our study shows that PBA is particularly suited for the molecular dissection of lateral root development in maize and suggests that PBA does not mimic known molecular boron deficiency responses.

works.title: SlJRE4-SlTPP1 confers carbon starvation tolerance by inhibiting starch degradation in tomato leaves at night
works.abstract: Under carbon starvation, plants have evolved a precise regulatory network governing starch degradation rates to avert excessive depletion of starch reserves, thereby sustaining carbon homeostasis and prolonging survival. We previously found that overexpression of the trehalose-6-phosphate phosphatase gene SlTPP1 slows nocturnal starch degradation in tomato leaves under neutral-day conditions; however, its function and regulatory mechanism underlying leaf starch degradation under low light (LL)-induced carbon starvation remain elusive. Here, we demonstrate that SlTPP1 slows nocturnal starch degradation in tomato leaves under carbon starvation. SlTPP1 overexpression suppresses nocturnal starch degradation and inhibits β-amylase activity in tomato leaves under neutral-day, short-day, and LL conditions. LL induces the expression of starch-degrading enzyme genes while concurrently upregulating SlTPP1 transcription in leaves. Furthermore, the jasmonate (JA)-responsive ethylene-responsive factor transcription factor SlJRE4 directly binds to the GCC-box cis-element in the SlTPP1 promoter and activates its expression. SlJRE4 transcription is also induced by LL. SlJRE4 overexpression similarly slows nocturnal starch degradation and represses β-amylase activity in leaves under neutral-day, short-day, and LL conditions. Additionally, exogenous methyl jasmonate under LL inhibits leaf starch degradation and upregulates the expression of SlJRE4 and SlTPP1. LL upregulates the expression of JA biosynthesis genes and elevates JA levels in tomato leaves. Moreover, SlTPP1 overexpression indirectly enhances SlJRE4 expression in leaves. Collectively, our findings uncover that the SlJRE4-SlTPP1 module acts as a braking mechanism to attenuate the rapid starch degradation in leaves triggered by LL-induced carbon starvation, representing a critical adaptive strategy for plants to improve survival under carbon starvation stress.

works.title: Loss of splicing factor SR45 reshapes tissue-dependent alternative polyadenylation landscapes and transcriptome responses to salt in Arabidopsis
works.abstract: Serine/arginine-rich 45 (SR45) is a plant-specific SR-like splicing factor and an RNA-binding protein involved in Arabidopsis development and stress responses. Although SR45 has been primarily studied for its role in pre-mRNA alternative splicing (AS), whether it also regulates alternative polyadenylation (APA) remains unclear. Here, we combined poly(A) tag sequencing (PAT-seq) and RNA-seq to examine APA, AS, and gene expression in wild-type (WT) and sr45-1 plants across inflorescence, leaf, and root under normal conditions, and in leaf and root under prolonged mild salinity. Under normal conditions, SR45 loss caused widespread changes in poly(A) site usage, with distal site shifts occurring more frequently than proximal shifts across tissues. APA, AS, and differential gene expression showed only partial overlap, with significant enrichment between APA and AS but not with gene expression changes, indicating that APA represents a distinct layer of SR45-mediated transcriptome regulation. Under prolonged mild salinity conditions, pairwise analyses showed preference of distal poly(A) site usage in WT and proximal site usage in sr45-1, particularly in leaf. Replicate-aware genotype-by-treatment interaction analyses further identified genotype-dependent differences in APA and gene expression, where more genotype-treatment interacting genes detected in leaf than in root. Genes encoding polyadenylation and splicing factors also showed changes in APA, AS, or transcript abundance. Together, these results expand the known role of SR45 from splicing regulation to APA-associated transcriptome remodeling and reveal that SR45 is required for proper salt-responsive changes in transcript abundance in Arabidopsis.

works.title: The art of multi-tasking: plant responses to their environment
works.abstract: Plant growth, development and survival are a continuous balancing act, integrating numerous environmental signals with core developmental programs. Nevertheless, in plant physiological research we usually study responses to the environment one factor at the time. It was the advent of microarray-based transcriptomics, and specifically the demonstration that combined treatments produce unique transcriptional signatures, that transformed stress combination into a defined molecular research program. We highlight how the field has evolved from the first seminal reports that combined severe abiotic stress treatments to a more comprehensive understanding of plant response to a range of conditions, including temperature, water availability, nutrients and light. We propose to broaden the conceptual framework from "combined stress" to a more inclusive consideration of context-dependent integration of environmental signals into responses. Integration of dose-, time- and location-dependent responses to the key plant hormones auxin, abscisic acid, ethylene and jasmonate are discussed. To further this research domain, we recommend accurate recording of environmental conditions and routine incorporation of treatment gradations, from mild to severe, in our research. Realizing this integrative view will require combining data-rich omics and machine-learning approaches with focused, hypothesis-driven experiments.

works.title: The E3 ligase PpMBR2 targets PpABI5 for degradation and negatively regulates cold tolerance in peach fruit
works.abstract: Abscisic acid (ABA) is known to alleviate chilling injury (CI) of peach fruit, but the molecular mechanisms is poorly understood. Here, a regulatory module that mediates peach fruit CI response at both transcriptional and post-translational levels was identified. ABA induced the gene expression and protein accumulation of abscisic acid-insensitive 5 (PpABI5). In turn, PpABI5 stimulated the expression of genes involved in proline and flavonoid biosynthesis, antioxidant defense, and fatty acid desaturation. Transient and ectopic overexpression of PpABI5 enhanced cold tolerance in peach and tomato fruit, accompanied by elevated proline and flavonoid biosynthesis, enhanced antioxidant capacity, and fatty acid desaturation. PpABI5 interacted with an E3 ligase MED25-binding RING-H2 protein2 (PpMBR2), which ubiquitinated PpABI5 at the specific site of K140, thereby modulated its degradation and attenuated PpABI5-mediated transactivation of target genes. PpMBR2-overexpression aggravated fruit CI, whereas PpMBR2-silencing produced the opposite effect. Furthermore, PpABI5 interacted with an ethylene response factor CRF3 (PpERF-CRF3), and this interaction enhanced their transcriptional regulation of target genes. Collectively, the results reveal a dynamic regulatory module PpMBR2-PpABI5-PpERF-CRF3 that governs cold tolerance in peach fruit by regulating proline and flavonoid biosynthesis, antioxidant defense and fatty acid desaturation. These findings advance our understanding of phytohormone crosstalk and site-specific ubiquitination modification in fruit CI.

works.title: A brake for pathogen-induced reactive oxygen species burst
works.abstract: Marcella Teixeira; A brake for pathogen-induced reactive oxygen species burst, Plant Physiology, , kiag813, https://doi.org/10.1093/plphys/kiag813

works.title: JrTTG2 confers drought tolerance in walnut via the JrGSTU8 -mediated antioxidant pathway and interaction with JrEPSIN1
works.abstract: Drought significantly limits the productivity and quality of Juglans regia, yet the regulatory mechanisms governing drought tolerance in this economically vital nut tree remain largely elusive. Here, we report that the WRKY transcription factor JrTTG2 acts as a central hub in the walnut drought response by integrating transcriptional and protein-interaction networks. We identified JrTTG2 as a hypersensitive early-response gene, exhibiting a robust 333-fold induction in walnut roots under drought stress. Ectopic expression of JrTTG2 in Arabidopsis and poplar significantly enhanced drought tolerance, primarily by maintaining root architecture, increasing biomass, and reducing oxidative damage. Conversely, RNAi-mediated silencing of PagTTG2 in poplar led to stunted root systems and compromised antioxidant defense under water deficit. Transcriptomic and molecular analyses revealed that JrTTG2 directly binds to the W-box in the promoter of the JrGSTU8 gene to activate its transcription, thereby facilitating ROS scavenging. Furthermore, yeast two-hybrid and BiFC assays demonstrated that JrTTG2 physically interacts with the vesicle trafficking protein JrEPSIN1. Both JrGSTU8 and JrEPSIN1 showed highly synchronized induction with JrTTG2 in walnut roots during drought. Taken together, this study provides a novel dimension to the molecular mechanisms of woody plant adaptation and offers a promising candidate gene for breeding drought-tolerant walnut varieties.

works.title: Apoplastic sugars regulate stomatal opening and closure through integrated osmotic and metabolic mechanisms
works.abstract: The role of sucrose in stomatal regulation has been debated for more than a century, yet its underlying mechanism remains incompletely understood. Recent evidence indicates that apoplastic sucrose acts as a mesophyll-derived signal promoting stomatal opening in Arabidopsis, yet whether this mechanism operates in other species and under fluctuating environmental conditions, how sugars contribute to stomatal closure, and to what extent these responses depend on sucrose uptake and metabolism within guard cells (GCs) remain unresolved. Here, we carried out stomatal, metabolomics, and modeling analyses in leaves, the leaf apoplast, and GCs from tobacco wild-type and antisense lines for the GC SUCROSE TRANSPORTER 1 (NtSUT1). Daily variation in stomatal conductance (gs) was associated with the accumulation of sugars and organic acids in the apoplast. Stomatal opening and closure were associated with low and high concentrations of apoplastic sucrose over the diel course, respectively. Sugar feeding accelerated stomatal opening and closure in dark and light-adapted leaves, respectively, both in a concentration-dependent manner. NtSUT1 displayed alterations in apoplast and GC metabolite profiles, which resulted in lower gs and impaired sucrose-induced stomatal closure, compared with tobacco wild-type. Our findings suggest that apoplastic sugars and organic acids are associated with diurnal gs dynamics and that sugars can accelerate both stomatal opening and closure through an osmotic mechanism in the apoplast, and are also dependent on sucrose import and degradation within GCs. These results extend current models of stomatal regulation by demonstrating that sugars regulate both stomatal opening and closure through integrated osmotic and metabolic mechanisms.

works.title: Cell-cycle-driven epigenetic resetting maintains meristematic cell fate for shoot branching
Remaking wheat with a thousand cuts
Phloem conductivity decrease over 300 million years of fern evolutionary history
Natural variation in the evolutionarily conserved F‐box gene SDEF promotes seed dormancy in rice
works.abstract: SUMMARY Insufficient seed dormancy causes pre‐harvest sprouting (PHS) and severe yield losses in rice; however, genetic resources with practical breeding value remain limited. Here, we isolated a major dormancy gene, SDEF , via map‐based cloning using chromosomal single segment substitution lines (SSSLs), identifying a functional SNP (Arg‐to‐Trp) as the causal mutation. CRISPR/Cas9‐mediated knockout of SDEF led to PHS susceptibility, while overexpression significantly enhanced dormancy. Importantly, SDEF enhanced seed dormancy without compromising grain yield in SSSLs, confirming it as a promising breeding target. Moreover, SDEF encodes an angiosperm‐conserved, nuclear‐localized F‐box protein and is preferentially expressed in the embryo, with expression increasing during seed maturation and declining upon germination. Mechanistically, protein interaction assays confirmed that SDEF recruits OSK1, with the Trp‐type SDEF K exhibiting a more stable interaction than the Arg‐type SDEF H . SDEF is induced by abscisic acid (ABA) and appears to promote seed dormancy through the ABA pathway by activating ABA signaling genes and repressing α‐amylase genes, as evidenced by the reduced ABA sensitivity of sdef mutants. Additionally, haplotype analysis revealed that natural variation in SDEF is associated with divergent dormancy levels, and reduced nucleotide diversity in cultivated rice indicates that SDEF was selected during domestication. Collectively, our results provide insights into the molecular basis of SDEF‐ mediated dormancy, providing an ideal target for breeding PHS‐resistant rice.

works.title: OsYchF1 suppresses OsEF1Bγ ‐mediated ER detoxification to co‐involve the growth‐maintenance trade‐off in rice
works.abstract: Translation elongation is a fundamental biological process, yet its direct role in stress adaptation remains unclear. In this study, we uncover a novel regulatory axis in rice involving the unconventional G protein OsYchF1, which gates the detoxification activity of the elongation factor 1Bγ (OsEF1Bγ) in the endoplasmic reticulum. OsEF1Bγ is a subunit of the eEF1B complex and possesses an N-terminal glutathione S-transferase (GST) domain. We demonstrate that overexpression of OsEF1Bγ enhances rice tolerance to osmotic and saline stress by lowering malondialdehyde levels, suggesting its role as a positive regulator via GST-mediated detoxification. Conversely, we found that OsYchF1 interacts with OsEF1Bγ across multiple domains. This interaction competitively inhibits the binding of reduced glutathione to OsEF1Bγ by approximately 40-fold, thereby suppressing its GST activity in vitro. Consistently, OsYchF1 knockout mutants phenocopy OsEF1Bγ overexpressors, displaying enhanced stress tolerance, reduced reactive oxygen species accumulation, and increased antioxidant enzyme activities. Furthermore, we show that stress-induced downregulation of OsYchF1 acts as a physiological trigger, releasing this molecular brake to enable rapid activation of OsEF1Bγ-mediated detoxification in response to challenging environments. Collectively, our findings reveal a post-translational mechanism where OsYchF1 serves as a molecular brake on the ER-localized detoxification engine of OsEF1Bγ, fine-tuning abiotic stress adaptation and establishing an unexpected link between the translation machinery and cellular redox homeostasis.

works.title: Water stable isotopes reveal the ecohydrological importance of stemflow infiltration for mature and juvenile European beech
works.abstract: Stemflow of forest trees can contribute a significant fraction of water to forest's water fluxes; however, it is still unclear whether and to what extent trees and their neighbours use stemflow for water uptake and supply. We applied deuterium-enriched stemflow equivalent to a 23-mm throughfall event to adult Fagus sylvatica trees to trace stemflow through the soil and trees. We continuously measured in situ water stable isotopes in soil and xylem water and destructively sampled xylem water in the crowns of adult labelled, nonlabelled F. sylvatica and nonlabelled Picea abies, complemented by destructive xylem water sampling of neighbouring juvenile F. sylvatica. Stemflow water supported up to 5.7 ± 2.1% of daily sap flux of adult F. sylvatica trees labelled at the stem base and was detectable in xylem water for several weeks. In the soil, deuterium-enriched stemflow was present at a maximum distance of 0.40 m from the labelled tree. Moreover, nonlabelled juvenile trees within a distance of 2 m showed uptake of labelled water, indicating rooting into soil compartments affected by stemflow. We demonstrate the importance of stemflow as a water source for both adult and neighbouring juvenile F. sylvatica, even when soil water is not limiting.

works.title: A beneficial root endophyte buffers natural variation in pathogen susceptibility across Arabidopsis accessions
works.abstract: Host genetic diversity shapes pathogen susceptibility within plant populations, raising the question of whether beneficial root microbes can buffer these differences. The fungal root endophyte Serendipita indica (Si) promotes plant growth and can mitigate disease caused by the pathogen Bipolaris sorokiniana (Bs). Here, we assessed how natural host genetic variation influences Si-mediated protection against Bs in Arabidopsis thaliana. We screened 47 A. thaliana accessions for susceptibility to Bs with and without Si colonization and performed phenotypic, transcriptomic, and comparative genomic analyses of two genetically and geographically proximate Swedish accessions, T510 and T530, that differed strongly in Bs colonization. Si conferred consistent protection against Bs across all accessions, despite variation in baseline susceptibility and immune-gene content. T510 and T530 differed in Bs colonization, disease symptoms, transcriptional responses, and immune-gene repertoires, including presence-absence variation of the TIR-NLR gene ISI. T530 lacks ISI, and mutation of ISI in Col-0 increased Bs susceptibility, demonstrating that ISI contributes to root immunity. However, Si-mediated protection was retained in the absence of ISI, demonstrating that ISI is not required for this protective effect. Beneficial fungal endophytes can thus buffer phenotypic consequences of natural variation in pathogen susceptibility, stabilizing disease outcomes across genetically diverse plant populations.

works.title: RCD1 nuclear shuttling releases WRKY47 to trigger bHLH105 / bHLH115 ‐dependent iron acquisition
works.abstract: Iron (Fe) deficiency limits plant growth, yet its upstream regulatory mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we identify WRKY47 as a positive regulator of Fe-deficiency responses in Arabidopsis. WRKY47 directly binds and activates bHLH105 and bHLH115, key IVc bHLH factors that trigger the Fe uptake cascade. We further show that RCD1 interacts with WRKY47 and suppresses its DNA-binding and transcriptional activity. Fe deficiency also promotes the redistribution of RCD1 from the nucleus to the cytoplasm, suggesting a potential mechanism for modulating WRKY47 activity during the response. Our findings uncover a previously uncharacterized regulatory mechanism linking WRKY transcription factors and the bHLH cascade through RCD1-mediated modulation, providing a conceptual framework for engineering crops with enhanced Fe acquisition and stress resilience.

works.title: Decomposition and mycorrhizal suppression of saprotrophs remain stable after wildfire and clearcut disturbance in boreal forests
works.abstract: Boreal forests store a large portion of global terrestrial carbon, primarily in soils, yet their sensitivity to environmental changes remains uncertain. Disturbance is one major agent of change, with dominance shifting from wildfire to forest management over the past century. Mycorrhizal suppression of saprotrophic decomposition may be an important control on boreal soil carbon storage, but its occurrence and magnitude remain uncertain. Additionally, the distinct impacts of wildfire and clearcutting on decomposition and soil microbial communities remain largely unexplored. We quantified mycorrhizal suppression of saprotrophs and decomposition in needle and humus litter through a root-exclusion experiment in 31 sites across wildfire (4-375 yr since disturbance) and clearcut chronosequences (1-109 yr since disturbance) in northern Sweden. Mycorrhizas suppressed decomposition by 15.5 ± 5.9% overall, with no consistent change over time after disturbance. This pattern was linked to absolute fungal abundance but not to other microbial community shifts, soil temperature or soil moisture. Decomposition rates were stable across time since disturbance for all substrates and disturbance types. Our findings improve understanding of mycorrhizal-decomposition interactions and highlight the need to further explore key fungal traits and compositional changes, especially at the soil surface, that regulate carbon storage dynamics in boreal soils.

works.title: DELLA proteins modulate responsive and buffered transcriptional programs in Arabidopsis and rice roots under water limitation
works.abstract: Water limitation constrains plant growth and productivity, yet the molecular mechanisms regulating root responses remain incompletely understood. The DELLA repressors of gibberellin signaling are key growth regulators under stress, but their role in shaping transcriptional responses to water limitation, and its conservation, remain unclear. Here, we investigated DELLA function in roots of Arabidopsis thaliana and Oryza sativa under reduced water availability simulated by polyethylene glycol (PEG). Loss of DELLA function reduced the sensitivity of root growth to water limitation, affecting primary root elongation in A. thaliana and crown root formation in O. sativa. Transcriptomic profiling revealed extensive DELLA-dependent regulation, partitioned into two modes: (i) genes requiring DELLAs for appropriate responses to water limitation ("WT-responsive"), and (ii) genes whose responsiveness is detected predominantly in the absence of DELLAs ("buffered", an operational label for an expression pattern, not a demonstrated mechanism). These patterns suggest that DELLAs both enable specific responses and apparently constrain broader transcriptional responsiveness under osmotic stress. Although the requirement for DELLA function is conserved, the developmental outputs and downstream transcriptional programs are largely species-specific. Together, our results identify DELLAs as key modulators of root responses to water limitation, with a proposed dual role in shaping and limiting transcriptional dynamics.

works.title: CDC48 protein regulates the turnover of peroxisomal catalase in tobacco
works.abstract: In plant cells, protein homeostasis is tightly regulated to prevent imbalances between protein synthesis and degradation that can lead to proteotoxic stress. Protein turnover is largely maintained by the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS), with the AAA+ ATPase CDC48 facilitating the extraction and processing of ubiquitinated substrates. Previous studies identified redox-related proteins as plant CDC48 partners. Here, using tobacco cell lines overexpressing CDC48, we identified the peroxisomal catalase CAT1 as a substrate of CDC48-dependent turnover. CDC48 overexpression markedly reduced CAT1 abundance and activity, indicating post-translational regulation. CAT1 undergoes extensive polyubiquitination, and was rapidly degraded in a CDC48-dependent manner. Inhibition of deubiquitinating enzymes or CDC48 ATPase activity both led to the accumulation of ubiquitinated CAT1. Finally, CDC48 overexpression, which leads to reduced CAT1 levels, correlated with impaired peroxisomal function. These findings reveal a role for CDC48 in regulating peroxisomal protein turnover in tobacco.

works.title: PHYA and PHYC as Candidate Loci for Flowering Time and Developmental Plasticity in Wheat
works.abstract: Plant architecture and developmental timing are influenced by light availability, especially in high-density cropping systems, where canopy shading modifies both light intensity and spectral quality. Despite their ecological and agronomical importance, the genetic basis of these responses in wheat remains poorly understood. Here, using a Recombinant Inbred Lines (RILs) population, we investigated phenological and morphological traits under sunlight and simulated canopy shade. We identified a major QTL on chromosome 5A with light-dependent allelic effects, indicating genotype-by-environment variation in developmental responses. This QTL corresponds to a structural rearrangement, consistent with an inversion in the wild emmer reference genome that suppresses recombination and maintains a haplotype block at a flowering locus including PHYTOCHROME C (PHYC-A) and VERNALIZATION-1 (VRN-A1). Analysis of a tetraploid wheat diversity panel further showed that natural variation at PHYC-A interacted with VRN-A1 to regulate heading time, with the effect of PHYC-A being substantially stronger in winter VRN-A1 backgrounds. This epistatic interaction likely reflects PHYC's role in modulating the circadian phase of photoperiod-pathway genes. Additionally, we found an early stop codon in the BB genome copy of PHYTOCHROME A (PHYA-B) on chromosome 4B associated with delayed heading, supported by TILLING-derived phytochrome mutants that reveal distinct and complementary roles for PHYA and PHYC in regulating flowering time, plant height, and leaf elongation under simulated canopy shade. Our findings highlight the potential contribution of phytochrome variation to wheat development under canopy-like light environment, thereby extending model insights to agronomically relevant conditions.

works.title: VvSnRK1‐Mediated VvMYBC2‐L1 Phosphorylation in Repressing Anthocyanin Accumulation Under High Temperature in Grapevine
works.abstract: Global climate change has aggravated heat stress throughout the grape growing season, which reduces anthocyanin accumulation and impairs fruit quality. The molecular mechanisms by which high temperature inhibits anthocyanin biosynthesis have yet to be fully elucidated. In this study, we demonstrated that MYBC2-L1 functions as a transcriptional repressor and its expression is strongly induced under high-temperature conditions. MYBC2-L1 represses anthocyanin synthesis by downregulating the transcription of key structural genes in the biosynthetic pathway of VvUFGT (UDP-glucose: flavonoid 3-O-glucosyltransferase) and VvLDOX (leucoanthocyanidin dioxygenase). Further biochemical assays revealed that MYBC2-L1 physically interacts with sucrose non-fermenting 1-related protein kinase 1α (SnRK1α), a negative regulator of anthocyanin accumulation. SnRK1α catalysers the phosphorylation of MYBC2-L1 at the Ser51 (S51) residue to modulate its biological activity. Collectively, we have identified a novel VvMYBC2L1-VvSnRK1α regulatory module that integrates abscisic acid (ABA) and heat signalling pathways, thereby synergistically suppressing anthocyanin accumulation in grape berries.

works.title: Verticillium dahliae CFEM Effector VdCR Stabilises the Susceptibility Factor GhAGP31 to Suppress Host Vascular Immunity and Promote Cotton Verticillium Wilt
works.abstract: Plant pathogenic fungi secrete a wide array of effector proteins to manipulate host immunity, including those containing CFEM (Common in Fungal Extracellular Membranes) domains. Here, we identified a CFEM domain-containing effector VdCR from Verticillium dahliae, the causal agent of cotton Verticillium wilt. The expression of VdCR was drastically upregulated during cotton infection. Targeted deletion of VdCR compromised fungal oxidative stress resistance and pathogenicity on cotton, establishing it as a key virulence factor. VdCR physically targets cotton non-classical arabinogalactan protein GhAGP31 via its CFEM domain. Virus-induced gene silencing (VIGS) of GhAGP31 significantly enhanced reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation, callose and lignin deposition, and plant resistance to V. dahliae, confirming that GhAGP31 acts as a negative regulator of vascular immunity. In addition, we identified GhAGP31 as a negative regulator of cotton vascular development, revealing its dual roles in coordinating plant immunity and development. We further verified that VdCR stabilises GhAGP31 to promote its accumulation both in vitro and in planta. Collectively, this study demonstrates that GhAGP31 functions as a novel cotton susceptibility factor that suppresses both vascular immunity and development and can be stabilised by the V. dahliae CFEM effector VdCR to facilitate fungal infection.

works.title: Genome‐Wide Splicing Landscapes Across Poplar Cultivars Reveal a GBF3 ‐Mediated Post‐Transcriptional Switch Modulating Monolignol Biosynthesis
works.abstract: Black poplars (Populus deltoides, P. nigra, and their hybrids) represents economically and ecologically vital hardwood taxa characterised by rapid biomass accumulation, superior wood properties, and wide adaptability. However, the post-transcriptional regulatory mechanisms orchestrating xylem development in these perennial trees remain poorly understood. Here, we systematically profiled transcriptome and alternative splicing (AS) dynamics in the developing xylem across five representative cultivars: P. euramericana 'Zhonglin46' (Pe1), P. euramericana 'Guariento' (Pe2), P. nigra 'N179' (Pn1), P. deltoides 'Danhong' (Pd1), and P. deltoides 'Nanyang' (Pd2). RNA-seq analysis of 20 independent xylem libraries revealed 9,981 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and 6,638 alternatively spliced genes across 10 pairwise comparisons. Functional enrichment indicated that transcriptional variations primarily coordinates cell wall biosynthesis and cytoskeleton organisation, whereas AS preferentially tunes nucleic acid binding and metabolic processes. Regulatory network modelling positioned key AS events upstream of core xylogenesis cascades. Crucially, we identified the G-box binding factor GBF3 as a master splicing-regulated hub during secondary vascular differentiation. An intron retention event in GBF3 yields a truncated isoform with aberrant subcellular localisation and abolished DNA-binding capacity, which impairs its transcriptional repression of key lignin biosynthetic genes (PAL2, CAD1, and CCoAOMT2). Collectively, these high-resolution transcriptional and post-transcriptional landscapes illuminate the regulatory architecture of wood formation and provide a valuable genomic resource for trait improvement in woody perennials.

works.title: bZIP‐Mediated Activation of a Late Embryogenesis Abundant Protein MsLEA2 Enhances Aluminium Tolerance in Medicago sativa
works.abstract: The phytohormone abscisic acid (ABA) is rapidly induced in roots exposed to aluminium (Al) stress, yet the mechanisms by which it modulates Al-detoxification genes remain elusive. Here we uncover a hierarchical ABA-responsive regulatory network that orchestrates a Late Embryogenesis Abundant (LEA)_2 protein MsLEA2, which modulates Al tolerance in alfalfa (Medicago sativa L.). Using yeast one-hybrid (Y1H) assays, luciferase complementation imaging (LCI), mutagenesis, and electrophoretic mobility shift assays (EMSA), we show that three antagonistic bZIP transcription factors-MsABF2 (activator), MsDPBF3 (hyper-activator) and MsGBF1 (repressor)-dynamically regulate MsLEA2 expression through spatially distinct ABRE motifs, enabling precise transcriptional control. Functional analyses reveal that MsLEA2 acts as a multifunctional hub, that promotes (i) oxalate exudation via interactions with aquaporins (MsPIP2;1, MsPIP2;2, MsTIP1;1), (ii) reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavenging, and (iii) cell wall remodelling through binding to UDP-xylose synthase (MsUXS1). Golgi-targeted MsLEA2 facilitates apoplastic Al exclusion, a mechanism distinct from its cytoplasmic homologue AtLEA14, underscoring the importance of subcellular compartmentalisation in Al detoxification. Our findings establish LEA_2 proteins as pivotal components of secretory-pathway-mediated Al tolerance and provide actionable targets for engineering crops resilient to acidic soils.

works.title: Transcription Factor CsDOF3 Mediates Light‐Dependent Antagonistic Regulation of Theanine and Catechin Accumulation in Tea Plants
works.abstract: Light intensity critically modulates the accumulation of secondary metabolites in tea plants (Camellia sinensis), yet the regulatory mechanisms that coordinate the opposing responses of theanine (a nitrogen-rich amino acid) and catechins (carbon-rich flavonoids) remain poorly understood. Here, we identify CsDOF3, a light-responsive DOF (DNA-binding with one finger) transcription factor, as a candidate regulator influencing both metabolic pathways. Across a light intensity gradient of 5000-15 000 lx, CsDOF3 expression increases with light intensity, correlating with decreased theanine and increased catechin accumulation. Functional analyses demonstrate that overexpression of CsDOF3 suppressed theanine biosynthesis while promoting catechin synthesis, whereas virus-induced gene silencing produced the opposite phenotype. Mechanistically, CsDOF3 binds to the promoters of CsTSI (theanine synthetase 1, a key theanine biosynthetic gene) and CsANS (anthocyanidin synthase, a catechin biosynthetic gene) in vitro, with opposite effects on their transcriptional activity in dual-luciferase assays. Collectively, these findings suggest that CsDOF3 is a candidate regulator linking light conditions to the accumulation of theanine and catechins, providing a framework for understanding light-mediated regulation of tea flavour-related metabolites.

works.title: Site‐Specific Functional Response of the Tibetan Plateau's Forests to Climate Change Over the Past 200 Years – A Tree‐Ring Isotope Perspective
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Global warming challenges forest resilience on the Tibetan Plateau by disrupting tree's physiological adjustments. However, understanding the physiological adjustments between autotrophic and heterotrophic metabolism under shifting moisture regimes remains challenging. We investigated 200‐year tree functioning across a moisture gradient using tree‐ring width and carbon isotope variation (δ 13 C) to indicate water stress, and the covariation between tree‐ring cellulose δ 18 O and δ 2 H (O▬H relationship) to indicate shifts in autotrophic and heterotrophic metabolism. The moist site exhibited strong and stable O▬H coupling, reflecting dominant hydroclimatic control, though recent droughts induced decoupling and reduced growth. In contrast, the semi‐arid site showed lower and variable O▬H relationship, reflecting repeated transitional functional state. The arid‐site forest showed increased growth due to recent wetting, yet persistent O▬H decoupling indicated ongoing physiological adjustments. Combined with the instrumental data, we found that O▬H coupling strength depended on site‐specific hydroclimatic baselines, appearing stronger in dry years at arid sites but in wet years at semi‐arid sites. Overall, our framework provides a quantitative, time‐resolved perspective on trees' physiological response across moisture regimes. The O–H relationship serves as an early‐warning tool for detecting forests undergoing functional shifts under ongoing climate change.

works.title: The SlLRR‐RLK94‐SlPti1a Module Enhances Salt Tolerance by Modulating Reactive Oxygen Species and Hormone Homoeostasis in Tomato
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Tomato ( Solanum lycopersicum ) is a globally cultivated crop of high economic and nutritional importance, yet its growth and productivity are severely threatened by soil salinization. Although leucine‐rich repeat receptor‑like kinases (LRR‐RLKs) are key environmental sensors, the mechanisms governing tomato salt tolerance remain elusive. Here, we demonstrate that the SlLRR‑RLK94 and its downstream interacting protein, the receptor‑like cytoplasmic kinase SlPti1a, form a functional plasma membrane complex that positively regulates salt tolerance in tomato. CRISPR/Cas9‑mediated knockout of SlLRR‑RLK94 or VIGS‑mediated silencing of SlPti1a markedly reduced salt tolerance, resulting in severe leaf chlorosis and restricted root growth under salinity. Disruption of this module severely compromised physiological defence systems, leading to excessive reactive oxygen species accumulation, altered antioxidant enzyme activities, and an elevated Na + /K + ratio caused by uncontrolled Na + buildup. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that loss of SlLRR‑RLK94 extensively reprogrammed metabolic networks under salt stress, impairing photosystem homoeostasis and suppressing the diterpenoid biosynthesis pathway. This transcriptional reprogramming led to an endogenous hormonal imbalance characterised by gibberellin deficiency and abscisic acid accumulation. Collectively, our findings elucidate the molecular mechanisms by which the SlLRR‑RLK94‑SlPti1a module coordinates ionic, oxidative, and hormonal homoeostasis, providing promising genetic targets for breeding salt‑tolerant tomato cultivars.

works.title: The PoSAP8/PoDREB2A‐PoDHN1 Module Enhances Thermotolerance in Paeonia ostii
works.abstract: Plant growth and development are tightly regulated by environmental conditions, and high-temperature stress has become a major threat to vegetative productivity. Tree peony (Paeonia ostii) is a highly valued ornamental plant widely cultivated across Asia and Europe. Although heat stress is known to severely impair its normal development, the underlying molecular mechanisms remain largely elusive. Here, we investigated the cellular, molecular and genetic basis of thermotolerance in P. ostii. Physiological analyses revealed that high temperature markedly suppressed growth by altering key leaf physiological parameters. Through transcriptome sequencing and expression profiling, we identified PoDHN1, a dehydrin-encoding gene markedly induced by heat stress. Silencing PoDHN1 significantly compromised thermotolerance. We further demonstrated that PoDREB2A, a DREB transcription factor, bound to a DRE motif within the PoDHN1 promoter. In addition, PoDREB2A acted as an upstream activator of PoDHN1 by activating the intact PoDHN1 promoter, thereby enhancing thermotolerance in tree peony. Importantly, we found that the stress associated protein PoSAP8 physically interacts with PoDREB2A and enhances its activation of PoDHN1 promoter. Collectively, our findings establish the PoSAP8/PoDREB2A-PoDHN1 regulatory module, which is activated by high temperature and functions as a positive regulator of thermotolerance in tree peony. This study advances our understanding of heat stress responses in woody plants and provides potential genetic targets for breeding heat-tolerant tree peony cultivars.

works.title: Carotenoid Cleavage Dioxygenase 8 Enhances Interspecific Facilitation in Maize‐Soybean Intercropping via Arbuscular Mycorrhiza Symbiosis Under Phosphate Limitation
works.abstract: Carotenoid Cleavage Dioxygenase 8 (CCD8) regulates strigolactone (SL) biosynthesis, which mediates the establishment of arbuscular mycorrhiza fungal (AMF) symbiosis. This symbiosis makes a major contribution in nutrient uptake, thereby improving crop productivity, mostly without the need for specific inoculation. Quantifying the extent of this contribution in typical intercropping systems remains challenging. A pot experiment was conducted using ZmCCD8 knockout (zmccd8), overexpression (ZmCCD8-OE), and wild type (WT) maize lines, grown in sole cropping or intercropping with soybean under low phosphate (LP) and control conditions. Intercropped ZmCCD8-OE and soybean showed a 61.9% higher overyielding effect, partially attributed to a 72.7% greater AMF colonisation rate in ZmCCD8-OE than WT counterparts under LP. Together with the greater root, AMF promoted P accumulation by 58% and 35% in the ZmCCD8-OE shoot and root, respectively. Conversely, intercropped zmccd8 conferred negative impacts under LP, corresponding to 47.6% and 63.4% less overyielding and AMF colonisation, respectively. Consistent with these results was differential expression of genes (CCD8, D14, CCaMK, CYCLOPS, RAM1, PT6/PT8) regulating AMF symbiosis and P uptake in maize and soybean. Collectively, ZmCCD8 enhances interspecific facilitation by stimulating root growth and AMF symbiosis, providing a genetic approach for higher crop productivity in intercropping systems without inoculation.

works.title: Correction: Advances in mutant characterization for detecting causal mutations in crop plants
Advances in the transcriptional regulation of seed vigor and its application in molecular breeding for rice
works.abstract: Rice seed vigor is a life-cycle trait whose performance after sowing depends on physiological capacity established during seed development, preserved during storage, and reactivated during germination and seedling establishment. Rather than functioning as isolated stage-specific pathways, transcriptional networks coordinate a series of transitions between protection and growth. During seed development, transcription factors establish embryo competence, reserve organization, desiccation tolerance, and proteostasis, thereby creating the physiological capacity for subsequent performance. During storage, ABA- and auxin-associated bZIP networks, including the OsARF12-OsbZIP23 and OsbZIP23-PER1A modules and SAG9-associated regulation, maintain longevity through antioxidant and protective processes; emerging salicylic acid-associated signaling further extends this hormone-redox regulatory framework. After imbibition, ABA-GA balance, sugar and energy signaling, reserve mobilization, reactive oxygen species homeostasis, and cell expansion determine the timing and uniformity of germination, while related regulatory modules support establishment under salinity, chilling, water deficit, and oxygen limitation. Importantly, current evidence varies substantially in strength: some regulators are directly supported by germination, longevity, dormancy, or stress-vigor phenotypes, whereas others remain developmental candidates inferred mainly from grain composition or seed-development traits. Field-emergence validation and natural-storage evidence also remain limited. We therefore propose that rice seed-vigor improvement should prioritize stage-appropriate regulatory alleles and precise modulation of transcription-factor activity, while jointly considering storability, dormancy and pre-harvest sprouting resistance, field establishment, yield, and grain quality.

works.title: NSP2 phosphorylation modulates HYL1 nuclear import via KETCH1 to promote miRNA biogenesis in Arabidopsis
works.abstract: MicroRNA (miRNA) biogenesis in plants relies on the precise nuclear-cytoplasmic trafficking of the HYL1 protein. Here, we report that the NITRILE-SPECIFIER PROTEIN 2 (NSP2) is a previously unrecognized component of the Arabidopsis miRNA pathway. Through yeast two-hybrid, BiFC, Co-IP, and genetic analyses, we demonstrate that NSP2 physically interacts with HYL1 and genetically suppresses hyl1-2. NSP2 overexpression increases global miRNA abundance. Mechanistically, NSP2 acts as an adapter that bridges the importin-β family member KETCH1 to HYL1, thereby regulating HYL1 nuclear import and dicing-body (D-body) assembly. Dephosphorylation of NSP2 at a conserved threonine (T314) strengthens KETCH1-HYL1 association and further enhances pri-miRNA processing. Our study establishes NSP2 as a phosphorylation-regulated scaffold that coordinates HYL1 nuclear trafficking and microprocessor assembly, and reveals critical roles for NSP2 in miRNA biogenesis.

works.title: Sorghum grain biofortification by SbSTP20 -mediated hexose influx and sub-aleurone thickening
works.abstract: Biofortification offers a sustainable solution to "hidden hunger, " yet the trade-off between grain yield and nutritional quality remains a persistent breeding bottleneck. Modern crop breeding emphasises the balance between high yield and nutritional values. Use of novel genes/alleles for grain quality lost during domestication and genetic improvement has been proven an efficient way to help achieve the dual goals. In sorghum, we report here the discovery of SbSTP20, encoding a sorghum monosaccharide transporter, as an essential component for biofortification by mediating the endosperm hexose influx and sub-aleurone (SA) thickness. SbSTP20 was ectopically expressed in sorghum developing grains and its expression levels were negatively associated with SA thickness. CRISPR edited Sbstp20 lines decreased the influx of hexoses, and exhibited thicker sub-aleurone layers and 6.6-7.5% higher grain protein and enriched micronutrients (Fe, Zn). SbSTP20thick natural variant increased sub-aleurone layer thickness and improved grain nutritional quality without altering grain size or thousand-grain weight. The SbSTP20thick allele was absent in 93% of modern improved lines, implying that the genomic region containing SbSTP20 showed a moderate selection signature. The metabolizable energy of SbSTP20thick containing sorghum lines was up to 6% higher than that of commercial corn standards in swine digestion and metabolism experiments. Reintroducing this haplotype via marker-assisted selection could provide a molecular strategy for nutritional enhancement.

works.title: CsVTT1, a PQ-loop vacuolar amino acid transporter, mediates vacuolar theanine storage in tea plant roots under nitrogen supply
works.abstract: Theanine, a unique and major nitrogen storage amino acid in tea plants, is responsible for the tea umami taste and confers numerous health benefits. Despite its importance, the molecular and cellular mechanisms regulating its biosynthesis and accumulation remain poorly understood. In this study, we identified a PQ-loop amino acid transporter, CsVTT1 (Vacuolar Theanine Transporter 1), through integrative analyses including yeast mutant library screening, along with correlation analysis between gene expression and theanine accumulation, and homologous gene complementation. Our findings revealed that CsVTT1 expression is nitrogen-inducible and strongly correlates with theanine accumulation in tea plant roots under different nitrogen regimes. Functional characterization in both yeast and Xenopus laevis oocytes demonstrated that CsVTT1 facilitates cytoplasmic to vacuolar transport of theanine, glutamine, arginine and other amino acids. Genetic manipulation experiments showed that CsVTT1 overexpression significantly enhanced theanine accumulation in tea plant roots, whereas its knockdown reduced theanine levels. Notably, CsVTT1 overexpression in rice greatly increased arginine accumulation, the main nitrogen storage amino acid in non-tea plants, suggesting a conserved role for CsVTT1 in nitrogen metabolism and storage, consistent with its newly identified function in mediating theanine storage in the vacuole. Consequently, CsVTT1 emerges as a promising target for genetic strategies aimed at simultaneously enhancing tea quality and nitrogen use efficiency.

works.title: 4-hydroxyphenethyl alcohol, a phenolic metabolite synthesized by GhADH1, positively regulates cotton fiber elongation
works.abstract: Cotton is the dominant natural fiber for global textiles, with fiber length being a critical determinant of quality and agronomic yield. While phytohormones and primary metabolism are known to affect fiber growth, secondary metabolism's regulatory roles remain poorly characterized. Here, we identify two medium-chain dehydrogenase/reductase (MDR) homeolog genes, GhADH1-A and GhADH1-D, highly expressed during the fiber elongation stage in Gossypium hirsutum (G. hirsutum). Functional analyses showed that GhADH1 knockout plants produced significantly shorter fibers and smaller bolls, whereas GhADH1 overexpression enhanced both traits. Metabolomic profiling revealed reduced levels of the phenolic alcohol 4-hydroxyphenethyl alcohol (4-HPEA) in fibers of GhADH1 knockout lines while overexpression lines contained enhanced 4-HPEA levels. LC-MS and in vitro enzymatic assays showed that GhADH1 catalyzes the conversion of 4-hydroxyphenylacetaldehyde (4-HPAA) to 4-HPEA. In vitro ovule culture assays showed that both 4-HPAA and 4-HPEA promote fiber elongation in a concentration-dependent manner, with 4-HPAA effect requiring GhADH1 activity. Transcriptomic profiling showed that GhADH1 overexpression and 4-HPEA treatment trigger consistent responses, with auxin signaling as the dominant regulatory hub. GhADH1 and 4-HPEA increased endogenous auxin levels in fibers, while auxin inhibitor treatments abrogated their elongation-promoting effects, confirming the pathway's dependence on auxin homeostasis. Together, these findings uncover a GhADH1-4-HPEA metabolic pathway positively regulating cotton fiber elongation by modulation of auxin homeostasis, revealing a new role for secondary metabolism in fiber development.

works.title: Transcriptional coordination of the aromatic amino acid metabolic network in Petunia and beyond
works.abstract: Plants produce vast arrays of specialized metabolites mediating ecological interactions, notably including phenylalanine-derived metabolites. Biosynthesizing these metabolites requires not only defined structural pathways, but also tight coordination between the shikimate pathway, aromatic amino acid production, and downstream specialized metabolism, such as benzenoid metabolism. Regulation occurs at multiple levels, including post-translational control of enzymes through mechanisms such as allostery, wherein binding of a regulatory metabolite alters catalytic activity. However, transcriptional regulation is also a flux control mechanism in these pathways and has increasingly been studied. Here, we summarize recent developments in this field. Petunia emerged as a key model for understanding how transcriptional networks regulate this metabolic system, complemented by discoveries in other species. Central to this regulation are MYB transcription factors, including PhODO1, PhEOBI, and PhEOBII, which coordinate the expression of genes involved in both precursor supply and volatile formation. These regulators operate within broad networks that integrate environmental signals, including light, circadian rhythms, temperature, and hormonal cues, through additional transcription factors. Developmental regulators, particularly MADS-box transcription factors, link floral organ identity with metabolism, ensuring scent production occurs within appropriate developmental stages and tissues. Beyond transcriptional and enzymatic regulation, accumulation and utilization are also influenced by post-synthetic processes, including glycosylation, intracellular sequestration, transport, storage, and export. Together, these elements form multilayered frameworks that coordinates primary and specialized metabolism, ultimately determining composition, accumulation, and utilization of specialized metabolites. Expanding this framework across plant species will be essential for understanding metabolic regulation and enabling targeted manipulation of aroma and stress-related traits in crops.

works.title: The SCHENGEN pathway regulates lignin barrier formation via the receptor-like cytoplasmic kinase BIK1 in plant immunity
works.abstract: Abstract Lignin deposition is a hallmark of plant immunity, forming a physical barrier that restricts pathogen spread and confines hypersensitive cell death. However, how immune signaling triggers this barrier remains unclear. Here, we show that the Casparian strip surveillance pathway is repurposed during effector-triggered immunity to control lignin barrier formation. The peptide ligands CIF1 and CIF2 and their receptor SGN3 are transcriptionally induced upon avirulent bacterial infection and are required for pathogen-induced lignification and disease resistance. Mechanistically, SGN3 directly interacts with and phosphorylates BIK1, which acts as the primary downstream receptor-like cytoplasmic kinase in immune signaling. Genetic and molecular analyses further reveal that NLR-driven CIFs-SGN3-BIK1 signaling cooperates with pattern-recognition receptor pathways to promote ROS production and lignin polymerization during ETI. These findings uncover a previously unrecognized immune function of the SGN pathway and establish a signaling module linking pathogen recognition to lignin-based barrier formation.

works.title: Directional water transport system resolves fertilization–dispersal conflicts in Marchantia
Sorghum Metabolic Atlas: A fluorescent protein‐based subcellular localization resource for sorghum enzymes
works.abstract: SUMMARY Plant metabolism drives traits essential for productivity and resilience, yet understanding metabolic networks requires subcellular, cellular, and tissue‐level spatial context that remains limited, particularly in crop species. Experimentally derived subcellular localization data for enzymes are sparse, constraining analyses of metabolic organization in the cell. We developed a high‐throughput protoplast transformation and fluorescent protein (FP) tagging system optimized for Sorghum bicolor , a climate‐resilient C 4 crop. Using this platform, we experimentally determined the subcellular localization of 234 metabolic enzymes spanning 184 pathways. The sorghum enzymes we characterized localize to 12 subcellular compartments. Comparison with computational predictions highlights variable accuracy across compartments, and cross‐species comparison with Arabidopsis thaliana shows partial agreement with available experimental data. All data are accessible through the Sorghum Metabolic Atlas ( www.sorghummetabolicatlas.org ) web platform, enabling search, visualization, and download. This study presents a large‐scale experimental dataset of enzyme localization in sorghum, providing a resource for studies of plant metabolic organization and comparative analyses.

This study converts the intrinsic regenerative capacity of alfalfa shoot tips and stem segments into a practical gene delivery and CRISPR/Cas9 editing system. By defining an early shoot-tip developmental window that minimizes chimerism and validating multiple target genes, cultivars, and explant types, this method provides a rapid callus-free platform for functional genomics and molecular breeding in polyploid perennial forage crops.

works.title: Issue Information
Deciphering the molecular basis of maize cold tolerance via integrative regulatory network analysis
works.abstract: Maize (Zea mays L.) is a globally critical but cold-sensitive crop. Understanding the temporal organization of cold-responsive, circadian-associated, and hormone-associated transcriptional programs is essential for deciphering how plants balance growth and survival under cold stress to ensure food security. We performed high-resolution time-series RNA-seq on 108 maize seedling samples across 14 time points (0-36 h cold stress and 24 h recovery). Coronatine (COR) was utilized as a defined JA-associated chemical perturbation to probe hormone-associated transcriptional responses during cold stress. We identified 12 986 cold-responsive and 2259 recovery-responsive genes, revealing a recovery-associated transcriptional transition characterized by suppressed photosynthesis-related processes and enrichment of genes associated with lipid catabolism, accompanied by transient physiological stress during early recovery. Cold stress induced widespread phase shifts and reduced oscillation amplitudes among circadian-associated transcripts, while COR identified distinct hormone-associated transcriptional modules and candidate network-associated genes, including ZmWRKY71 and ZmHSP28, whose roles were further supported by molecular and genetic analyses. This study establishes a temporally resolved transcriptional framework for maize cold stress and recovery, integrating transcriptional dynamics, physiological responses, and experimentally supported regulatory nodes.

works.title: Single‐cell transcriptome atlas reveals a WRKY33 ‐ HSP81 regulatory module that orchestrates phenylpropanoid‐mediated defense against Sclerotium rolfsii in Dendrobium officinale
works.abstract: Plants employ cell-type-specific transcriptional programs to defend against pathogens, yet the cellular heterogeneity of immune responses in the medicinal orchid Dendrobium officinale Kimura et Migo remains largely unexplored. A single-cell transcriptomic atlas of the D. officinale stem base upon Sclerotium rolfsii infection was constructed, profiling over 20 000 cells across 12 and 24 h post-infection. A total of 21 cell clusters were resolved into 6 major cell types-epidermal, ground tissue parenchyma, proliferating, xylem, phloem, and vascular bundle parenchyma cells-with identities validated by fluorescence in situ hybridization. Cell-type-specific analyses revealed that epidermal and phloem cells mounted early defense responses, while xylem cells exhibited the most extensive transcriptional reprogramming at 24 hpi, coinciding with the activation of lignin biosynthesis pathways. WRKY33 was identified as a central transcriptional activator that directly binds W-box motifs in the promoters of lignin biosynthetic genes C4H and HCT, promoting lignin deposition and enhancing disease resistance. Conversely, the nuclear-localized chaperone HSP81 physically interacts with WRKY33 and functions as a broad regulator of multiple transcription factors via co-factor sequestration, thereby compromising defense when overexpressed. These findings uncover a WRKY33-HSP81 regulatory module that orchestrates phenylpropanoid-mediated defense in D. officinale, providing a high-resolution cellular framework for understanding plant immunity and offering potential targets for improving disease resistance in this economically valuable species.

works.title: Nuclear importin α1 AtIMPA1 regulates stomatal reopening to defend against Pst DC3000 by orchestrating ABA signaling
works.abstract: Importin α family proteins serve as essential carriers for transporting specific disease-resistant proteins into the nucleus, enabling these proteins to function properly. However, whether importin α proteins are involved in plant immunity remains unclear. Here, we characterized a guard cell-expressed protein importin α1 AtIMPA1, which contributed to resistance against Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato DC3000 (Pst DC3000). When dip-inoculated with Pst DC3000, the impa1 mutants exhibited increased susceptibility, along with significant stomatal reopening induced by the phytotoxin coronatine (COR) secreted by Pst DC3000; while overexpression of AtIMPA1 enhanced resistance to Pst DC3000 with compromised stomatal reopening induced by COR. Notably, following syringe-infiltration of Pst DC3000, the impa1 mutants showed increased resistance, whereas overexpression lines were more susceptible to Pst DC3000, indicating that COR-triggered stomatal reopening is a primary determinant in AtIMPA1-mediated disease resistance. Further investigations revealed that AtIMPA1 regulated COR-triggered stomatal reopening is linked to abscisic acid (ABA) signaling. Mutation of AtIMPA1 attenuated the ABA-mediated inhibition of root length and seed germination, and disrupted the ABA-induced protein abundance and localization of the ABA-responsive protein, supporting its role in regulating the ABA response. These findings shed light on the functional significance of AtIMPA1 in COR-triggered stomatal reopening and provided new insights into how importin α proteins orchestrate ABA signaling to regulate plant immunity.

works.title: An efficient gene delivery method utilizing the regenerative capacity of alfalfa ( Medicago sativa )
works.abstract: Alfalfa (Medicago sativa), an autotetraploid species, is a globally important forage crop. Traditional genetic transformation methods predominantly rely on leaf-derived callus, a process that is complex, inefficient, and particularly challenging to generate stable transgenic lines in polyploid plants. To address these limitations, we developed an efficient transformation system that bypasses callus induction by directly exploiting stem regeneration. Our protocol enables the generation of stable gene-edited alfalfa plants from shoot tips. It accommodates stem explants from various developmental stages and significantly reduces the time required. Moreover, this approach was effective across multiple alfalfa cultivars, and preliminary proof-of-concept experiments in Nicotiana tabacum and Solanum lycopersicum suggested potential transferability beyond alfalfa. This study represents a substantial advancement in perennial plant transformation and provides a robust and practical platform for optimizing stem regeneration-based genetic modification systems.

works.title: Light‐induced phyB ‐ NPR1 interaction activates systemic acquired resistance
works.abstract: Summary Light perception by phytochromes controls different aspects of plant–environment interactions including plant immunity; however, the underpinning molecular mechanisms are less well‐understood. Upon localized attack on leaves by avirulent pathogens, the systemic accumulation of salicylic acid (SA) is required for the establishment of systemic acquired resistance (SAR) throughout the plant to curtail pathogen spread. We demonstrate that light‐mediated Small Ubiquitin‐like Modifier 1 (SUMO) conjugation to phytochrome B (phyB) is critical for increasing cellular SA levels to orchestrate SAR upon avirulent bacterial infection. SA promotes SUMOylation of phyB, which enables it to interact with the SA receptor, Nonexpressor of Pathogenesis‐Related 1 (NPR1) via its SUMO1‐interacting motif. SUMOylation of phyB is enhanced by the accumulation of SUMO‐Conjugating Enzyme (E2) (SCE1) and the degradation of SUMO protease Overly Tolerant to Salt 1 (OTS1) in SAR‐induced systemic tissues. Using confocal imaging, we show that SUMOylated phyB undergoes liquid–liquid phase separation together with NPR1 in nuclear bodies. We further validated through immunoprecipitation, ChIP and RNA‐seq analysis that SUMOylated phyB associates with NPR1 and TGA transcription factors in nuclear photobodies to induce the expression of PR1 gene. We reveal a post‐translational modification mechanism in which light‐induced SUMOylation of photoreceptors promotes SAR by regulating NPR1 function.

works.title: Tree and neighborhood damage have distinct effects on delayed mortality after a severe hurricane
works.abstract: Tropical forest resilience, biodiversity, and carbon sequestration depend on tree survival. Disturbance events, such as hurricanes, generate distinct forms of damage at the individual-tree and neighborhood scale, providing a unique setting to disentangle the causal contributions of mortality drivers. Leveraging post-hurricane census data for nearly 4000 trees in the Luquillo Forest Dynamics Plot, Puerto Rico, we used a causal inference framework combined with Bayesian multilevel models to estimate the effect of individual- and neighborhood-scale damage on delayed tree mortality following Hurricane Maria (2017). Individual damage effects depended on species identity and tree size. Stem break emerged as the most lethal form of damage across the community. Neighborhood damage was associated with elevated mortality following Hurricane Maria, independent of focal tree damage. This effect was strongest among large trees, consistent with disproportionately high physiological stress resulting from greater inherent metabolic demands, refoliation energy costs, and evapotranspiration following canopy recovery. Severe biomass loss (> 75% crown loss) buffered large trees from negative neighborhood effects, revealing a positive pruning effect on survival. Our study advances mechanistic understanding of delayed tree mortality, while also suggesting how mortality patterns may shift with expected increases in disturbance severity under a warming climate.

works.title: Trait‐based plant ecology: some history and some future
works.abstract: Since around the year 2000, trait-based ecology has become self-aware as a strand of research within ecology. How did this happen? What is trait-based ecology now? And where might it go in future? This paper offers selective answers to those questions. We first outline the history leading up to the emergence of trait-based plant ecology during the 1990s. Second, we assess briefly what has been achieved up to mid-2020s. Third, we discuss two challenges (among many) for trait-based plant ecology over the next 25 yr. One is about the boundaries of species ranges along temperature gradients. Some of these boundaries may be decided by thermal tolerance, others by biotic interactions such as competition or pathogens. How can we identify which applies to which species? Which traits, feasible to measure across many species, might help with this? A second major challenge is about the global zonation of vegetation physiognomy or biome types. How well can we explain this in terms of traits, and from first principles, meaning via eco-evolutionary models for why different trait values should be competent and competitive in different settings? First-principle rules for how ecosystems are constructed should be central to ecology as a discipline.

works.title: Polycistronic amiRNA ‐Mediated Multiplex Silencing of Clade A PP2Cs Confers Broad‐Spectrum Abiotic Stress Tolerance in Wheat
Mechanistic Insights into PTM-Mediated Architectural Rewiring of the Leaf Senescence Program
works.abstract: Leaf senescence is a highly coordinated developmental program essential for nutrient remobilization and plant fitness. While the underlying transcriptional and epigenetic landscapes have been extensively mapped, emerging evidence identifies post-translational modifications (PTMs) as the primary regulatory hubs providing the requisite sensitivity and precision for senescence signaling. This review systematically delineates the mechanistic contributions of diverse PTMs-including phosphorylation, ubiquitination, acetylation, methylation, glycosylation, lipidation, hydroxylation, S-nitrosylation, and oxidative PTMs-to the architectural rewiring of the senescence program. Rather than functioning merely as downstream effectors, PTMs operate as integrated "execution" and "decision-making" layers that bridge environmental inputs, hormonal fluxes, and metabolic status. By dynamically modulating key senescence-associated transcription factors (e.g., ORE1, WRKY53), kinase cascades, and autophagy-related networks, PTM registries facilitate the initiation, amplification, and irreversible commitment of leaf cells to senescence. Furthermore, we discuss how the interplay and crosstalk among distinct modification types establish a sophisticated combinatorial logic for sensing physiological thresholds. By integrating recent advances in single-cell proteomics and spatial omics, this synthesis highlights the paradigm shift toward cell-type-specific PTM atlases. Ultimately, these molecular insights provide a robust theoretical framework for the precision engineering of crop senescence to enhance resilience and yield.

works.title: CauYL, encoding a magnesium chelatase H subunit, is required for chlorophyll accumulation and normal leaf coloration in cauliflower
Correction: Discovery of a novel non-race-specific adult-plant resistance (APR) locus conferring stripe rust immunity in spelt wheat and its suppression in bread wheat
Low ambient temperatures regulate Arabidopsis abscisic acid signaling and seed germination via CBFs–ABI3/ABI5–ICE1 interactions
works.abstract: Seed germination is profoundly influenced by diverse environmental stimuli (e.g., temperatures), but the associated underlying molecular mechanisms remain largely uncharacterized. In this study, we demonstrated that low ambient temperatures, such as 16°C, suppress Arabidopsis thaliana seed germination, with endogenous abscisic acid (ABA) signaling revealed as a critical part of the underlying mechanism. The germination suppression and ABA response regulation by low ambient temperatures require ABSCISIC ACID INSENSITIVE3 (ABI3) and ABI5, two indispensable transcriptional activators in the ABA signaling pathway. In-depth analyses demonstrated physical associations between ABI3/ABI5 and low-temperature-responsive C-REPEAT BINDING FACTOR1 (CBF1), CBF2, and CBF3 (i.e., CBFs). Genetic evidence confirms that CBFs are essential for low-temperature- and ABA-mediated germination repression. Furthermore, CBFs and ABI3/ABI5 synergistically mediate the inhibitory effects of both low temperatures and ABA on germination. Mechanistically, these factors reciprocally enhance each other's transcriptional activities and promoter enrichment at downstream target genes. Notably, CBFs also directly bind INDUCER OF CBF EXPRESSION1 (ICE1), establishing an antagonistic regulatory axis with ABI5. Collectively, our findings underscore the critical modulatory effects of low ambient temperatures on ABA signaling and seed germination, thereby elucidating the mechanism by which the CBFs-ABI3/ABI5-ICE1 module functions as a signal transducer that converts environmental stimuli into endogenous hormone signals.

works.title: Allelic tuning of PtoRLK609 kinase activity shapes adaptive xylem remodeling in Populus tomentosa
works.abstract: Climate change poses unprecedented challenges to perennial trees. However, the molecular mechanisms by which trees achieve long-term adaptive xylem remodeling remain poorly understood. Here, using transcriptomics and population genomics in 302 Populus tomentosa accessions sampled from three climatically distinct subpopulations, we identified receptor-like kinases (RLKs) associated with climate-related variation in xylem lignification. Among 49 candidates, the wall-associated kinase PtoRLK609 showed among the strongest signatures of population differentiation, a pattern consistent with climate-associated selection. Two major PtoRLK609 haplotypes, defined by four linked missense variants, showed marked geographic differentiation, with PtoRLK609Hap2 reaching fixation or near-fixation in northern populations that experience drier and cooler climates, and was associated with elevated lignin content. PtoRLK609 phosphorylates the transcription factor PtoERF105 at Ser171, which promotes its nuclear accumulation and enhances activation of the lignin biosynthesis genes PtoLAC4 and PtoCCoAOMT1, as well as the vessel development regulator PtoVND7. The PtoRLK609Hap2 protein variant showed higher kinase activity and more efficient phosphorylation of PtoERF105 than PtoRLK609Hap1, linking natural protein variation to differential transcriptional output. Consistent with this mechanism, gain- and loss-of-function analyses showed that PtoRLK609 promotes secondary cell wall lignification, elevates the syringyl-to-guaiacyl (S/G) ratio, increases vessel density, and is associated with better maintenance of stem water status under controlled water deficit. These findings characterize a PtoRLK609-PtoERF105 phosphorylation module associated with xylem remodeling and identify an RLK locus that is a strong candidate for contributing to climate-associated divergence in perennial trees.

works.title: A homolog of Growth Regulating Factor Targets Protein Synthesis Genes to Regulate Seed Protein Accumulation in Soybean
works.abstract: Growth Regulating Factor (GRF) genes encode a family of highly conserved plant transcription factors that control diverse developmental processes. However, no GRF5 orthologs have been directly linked to seed protein accumulation. Here we demonstrate that GmGRF5a, a soybean homolog of GRF5, functions as a key positive regulator of seed protein accumulation. GmGRF5a is preferentially expressed in reproductive tissues, with transcript levels gradually increasing throughout seed development. Overexpression of GmGRF5a driven by its native promoter or the CAB3 promoter increased seed protein content by approximately one percentage point-comparable to the effect of known protein QTLs in soybean-without yield penalty across three independent field seasons, whereas CRISPR/Cas9-generated mutants showed reduced protein and oil contents. Integrative analysis of genome-wide DAP-seq and transcriptome profiling identified hundreds of direct GmGRF5a target genes significantly enriched in pathways related to protein synthesis, ribosomal biogenesis, and energy metabolism. Multiple independent molecular assays, including ChIP-qPCR, EMSA, and dual-luciferase reporter assays, confirmed that GmGRF5a directly activates genes encoding seed storage proteins (e.g., GmCupin1-1) and translational components (e.g., GmRPS4 and GmGOGAT2). Furthermore, natural variation at amino acid position 124 near the WRC DNA-binding domain is associated with seed protein content and exhibits a latitude-dependent distribution pattern consistent with regional breeding priorities. Our findings demonstrate that GmGRF5a coordinates a transcriptional network governing seed protein synthesis and highlight its potential as a promising target for breeding high-protein soybean cultivars without compromising agronomic performance.

works.title: Glutamate promotes cold tolerance through CsGLR3.2- and Ca2+-associated CBF signaling in tea plants
works.abstract: Low temperature limits the productivity and quality of tea plants, particularly when spring cold spells damage vulnerable young shoots. However, the metabolic signals that regulate C-repeat binding factor (CBF)-mediated cold responses remain unclear. Time-series metabolomic analysis revealed progressive glutamate accumulation in cold-treated tea shoots, accompanied by a marked decline in theanine content. Exogenous glutamate enhanced cold tolerance in tea shoots. By contrast, co-silencing of CsGGT2 and CsGGT4 attenuated cold-induced glutamate accumulation and compromised cold tolerance, indicating that CsGGT2/CsGGT4-associated theanine turnover contributes to cold-induced glutamate accumulation. Silencing CsGLR3.2 attenuated the protective effect of glutamate and reduced glutamate-enhanced CsCBF1-CsCBF4 expression. Pharmacological treatments provided complementary support for the involvement of GLR- and Ca2+-associated signaling in this response. Transcriptomic analysis further showed that glutamate altered the expression of genes associated with flavonoid biosynthesis and redox homeostasis. Collectively, these findings connect the characteristic theanine metabolism of tea plants with cold-responsive glutamate signaling and support a model in which glutamate enhances CsCBF expression through CsGLR3.2- and Ca2+-associated signaling. Glutamate metabolism and GLR-associated signaling therefore represent potential targets for improving cold tolerance in tea plants.

works.title: PlMYB51 and PlMYB1R1 switch PlABI5 - PlCesA6 function to regulate seed dormancy and germination in Paeonia lactiflora
works.abstract: Seed dormancy is a key strategy for plants to adapt to fluctuating environments and ensure population propagation. Paeonia lactiflora seeds exhibit typical double dormancy, characterized by a prolonged germination cycle and low emergence rate that severely restrict their large-scale propagation. Although ABI5, the core transcription factor (TF) in the abscisic acid (ABA) signaling pathway, acts as a critical hub in maintaining seed dormancy, its upstream dynamic regulatory mechanism and downstream cell-wall-related target genes remain largely unknown. In this study, two upstream regulators of PlABI5, PlMYB51 and PlMYB1R1, were identified via yeast one-hybrid screening, and their regulatory mechanism was characterized. The results showed that both PlMYB51 and PlMYB1R1 belonged to the R2R3-MYB family. When acting alone, they directly bound to and activated the PlABI5 promoter, inhibiting seed germination. Upon forming a protein complex in the nucleus, their regulatory function was reversed and they repressed PlABI5 transcription to promote germination, supporting a proposed monomer activation-complex inhibition switch model. Furthermore, PlABI5 specifically targeted the PlCesA6 promoter and inhibited its expression without affecting the homolog PlCesA3. PlCesA6 positively regulated seed germination by promoting hypocotyl cell elongation, and its overexpression rescued the inhibition caused by PlMYB51/PlMYB1R1 overexpression. Collectively, this study proposes a working model for the PlMYB51/PlMYB1R1-PlABI5-PlCesA6 cascade in controlling seed dormancy and germination, and identifies a putative functional switching mode of MYB TFs mediated by protein-protein interactions. These findings provide key gene resources and a theoretical basis for artificial dormancy breaking and molecular breeding in P. lactiflora.

works.title: SmartPE enables efficient prime editing in dicot crops
Author Correction: Cell-based CRISPRa screen identifies a papillae-specific receptor kinase mediating broad-spectrum fungal resistance in rice
Author Correction: N-myristoylation-mediated shuttling of TaMP from plasma membrane to chloroplasts increases wheat susceptibility to rust fungi
DNA ‐Barcoded Polysaccharide Specific Monoclonal Antibodies Facilitate Sensitive and Multiplexed Detection of Cell Wall Polymers
works.abstract: Plant cell walls are polysaccharide-rich extracellular matrices composed of multiple complex carbohydrate polymer networks, including cellulose, hemicelluloses, pectins, and glycosylated proteins. Polysaccharide deposition critically impacts cell wall structure, and structural microheterogeneity within cell wall glycans also influences polymer rigidity and polymer-polymer interactions. Collections of monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) have been developed to target unique carbohydrate epitopes within cell wall polysaccharides and to investigate how these structural changes impact cellular and plant development.
