Here, we implement generalizable methods to attach unique DNA barcodes to mAbs that recognize major cell wall polysaccharide classes. By applying these mAbs individually to polysaccharide standards, we demonstrate that bound DNA barcoded antibody abundance can be measured via quantitative PCR. Additionally, we demonstrate that DNA-conjugated antibodies can be pooled to quantitatively analyze polysaccharide epitope composition of polysaccharide standards and fractionated cell wall material by amplifying their unique barcodes via qPCR. These results demonstrate that barcoded polysaccharide-directed mAbs offer sensitive, quantitative insights into cell wall polysaccharide composition and facilitate multiplexed profiling of cell wall polysaccharide abundance. This approach will also enable multiple future high-throughput applications, such as glycome profiling, spatial glycomics, and glycan interaction measurements, that will further our understanding of cell wall compositional impacts on plant physiology.

works.title: Lessons From CABBI : Advancing Vegetative Oil Production in C 4 Crops Through a Vertically Integrated DBTL Framework
works.abstract: ABSTRACT The global demand for renewable liquid fuels and biobased chemicals has intensified interest in engineering high‐biomass C 4 grasses to accumulate triacylglycerol (TAG) in vegetative tissues. Achieving this goal requires coordinated solutions across molecular biology, crop science, chemical engineering, and life cycle assessment, disciplines that rarely operate within a single research program. The Center for Advanced Bioenergy and Bioproducts Innovation (CABBI) was established to provide this integration through a Design–Build–Test–Learn (DBTL) framework applied to three C 4 feedstocks: saccharum ( Saccharum spp. hybrids), sorghum ( Sorghum bicolor ), and miscanthus ( Miscanthus × giganteus ). Through iterative DBTL cycles, CABBI has produced transgenic saccharum and sorghum lines with substantially elevated levels of vegetative TAG, with multi‐location field trials having confirmed stable trait heritability and lipid yields. We have also leveraged our integration to develop a dual system biorefinery that co‐recovers vegetative lipids with fermentable sugars at levels sufficient to achieve industrial ethanol titres. Importantly, this fully integrated cross‐disciplinary data integration model has highlighted the key constraints currently preventing TAG‐rich vegetative oil from achieving commercial viability as: (i) active lipid turnover, (ii) photosynthetic trade‐offs, (iii) spatial misexpression, and (iv) bioprocessing challenges. CABBI uses emerging technologies, including biofoundry‐enabled construct screening, precision genome editing, and machine‐learning‐assisted regulatory design, to further accelerate DBTL cycles. More broadly, this work illustrates how integrative centre‐scale research that unites diverse expertise can accelerate discovery and translation, positioning these systems to expand agricultural markets and contribute to a more secure and resilient bioeconomy.

works.title: Spatiotemporal Transcriptomics Reveals That a ZF‐HD– GmCWINV4 Module Controls Carbon Partitioning and Seed Size in Soybean
works.abstract: Seed size and oil content are key determinants of agronomic productivity in soybean (Glycine max). Although the ultrastructure and cellular composition of soybean seeds have been well characterised, the spatiotemporal expression patterns of genes governing sucrose transport and catabolism across distinct cell types remain poorly understood. Here, we present a high-resolution spatiotemporal transcriptomic atlas of early soybean seed development, spanning the globular, heart, and cotyledon stages. We delineated 17 distinct cell types and identified 249 cell-type marker genes. We further characterised the phloem region of the seed coat, a key compartment associated with sucrose transport and metabolism. Systematic profiling of sugar-related genes revealed cluster-specific and developmental stage-dependent transcriptional patterns. We functionally characterised GmCWINV4, a phloem-specific cell wall invertase that hydrolyses sucrose into glucose and fructose. Overexpression of GmCWINV4 substantially increased seed size, weight, and oil content in soybean. We also identified two zinc finger homeodomain (ZF-HD) transcription factors, GmZF-HD27 and GmZF-HD36, that directly activate GmCWINV4 transcription by binding to 'ATTA' cis-elements in its promoter. Moreover, we demonstrated that sucrose acts as an upstream signal that induces GmZF-HD36 transcription in a dose-dependent manner. Collectively, these findings provide a comprehensive spatiotemporal transcriptomic resource for studying soybean seed development and reveal a previously unreported ZF-HD-GmCWINV4 regulatory module that modulates post-phloem sucrose metabolism, thereby contributing to increased seed size and oil content. These findings offer mechanistic insights and potential targets for improving seed yield and nutritional quality in soybean.

works.title: Natural Variation in CYCLIC NUCLEOTIDE‐GATED ION CHANNEL 16 Controls Fruit Weight in Tomato
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Fruit weight is a crucial agronomic trait influencing yield and quality in tomato domestication. Although numerous quantitative trait loci (QTLs) controlling fruit weight have been reported, the underlying molecular mechanisms remain largely unresolved. Here, we identify natural variation in the promoter region of CYCLIC NUCLEOTIDE‐GATED ION CHANNEL 16 ( CNGC16 ) associated with both fruit weight and gene expression differences via genome‐wide association study (GWAS) in tomato accessions. Geographical and subpopulation analyses reveal that the large‐fruit CNGC16 haplotype was selectively favoured during domestication and may contribute to local environmental adaptation. Functional assays demonstrate that CNGC16 regulates fruit weight by promoting cell division and maintaining cytosolic Ca 2+ homeostasis in fruit cells. Mechanistically, CNGC16 physically and genetically interacts with calmodulin 6 (CaM6) to mediate calcium signalling that controls fruit size. These findings uncover a novel calcium‐dependent pathway regulating tomato fruit weight and propose CNGC16 and CaM6 as promising molecular targets for crop improvement.

works.title: S-nitrosoglutathione reductase deficiency is associated with altered recovery from repeated climate stress across generations in Arabidopsis thaliana
works.abstract: Climate change exposes plants to recurrent and interacting stresses, yet the extent to which these effects persist across generations, and the mechanisms involved, remain unclear. Here, we compared Arabidopsis thaliana wild type (WT, Col-0) plants with gsnor1-3 (hereafter, gsnor-ko), a mutant deficient in S-nitrosoglutathione reductase (GSNOR), an enzyme involved in nitric oxide homeostasis. Plants were propagated for three successive generations (G1-G3) under control, drought, elevated CO2, O3, heat (warm temperature), and combined treatment scenarios, followed by two recovery generations under control conditions (G4-G5). We quantified rosette growth, photosynthetic traits, seed production, and transcriptome dynamics by RNA-seq. Across environments, gsnor-ko exhibited reduced vegetative growth and reproductive output compared with WT. Transcriptomic responses were strongly scenario- and generation-dependent, with the largest differential expression shifts observed under heat and combined-treatment (combination) conditions. Compared with WT, gsnor-ko showed greater transcriptome similarity across generations and among genes differentially expressed in response to the same treatment. Functional enrichment and candidate-gene analyses identified pathways/components linked to DNA methylation, heterochromatin maintenance, histone ubiquitination, m6A RNA regulation, and methyl-donor metabolism. Together, these findings are consistent with a model in which GSNOR activity contributes to transcriptomic recovery after repeated climate stress, whereas GSNOR deficiency is associated with recurrent or reconfigured stress-associated transcriptional states at G1, G3, and G5, suggesting epigenetically associated regulatory reconfiguration.

works.title: The NopD effector of Bradyrhizobium XS1150 is phosphorylated by mitogen-activated protein kinases and promotes soybean nodulation
works.abstract: Effectors secreted by the rhizobial type III secretion system (T3SS) are host-specific determinants of nodule symbiosis. We previously showed that NopD from Bradyrhizobium sp. XS1150 possesses protease activity that negatively affects nodulation on Tephrosia vogelii. Using a NopD-calmodulin-dependent adenylate cyclase fusion expressed in Sinorhizobium sp. NGR234, we demonstrate translocation of NopD into nodule cells of Vigna unguiculata. In soybean, a nopD mutant of XS1150 induced fewer nodules than the wild-type strain. We found that NopD is a substrate of mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPKs) and identified four phosphorylation sites within its tandem repeat (TR) domain. In Arabidopsis protoplasts, NopD localized to nuclei and recruited co-expressed MAPKs to nuclear bodies. In tobacco cells, NopDΔTR and the phospho-dead NopD4A variant lost the ability to trigger NopD-induced cell death. Using a nopL-deficient Sinorhizobium sp. NGR234 strain expressing NopD, NopDΔTR or NopD4A, we found that only NopD suppressed premature senescence of bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) nodules. Further assays using a nopL knockout mutant of Sinorhizobium fredii USDA257 showed that NopD, but not NopD4A, enhanced nodulation in soybean. Together, these data establish NopD as a bona fide T3SS effector and show that its phosphorylation sites are required for effector activity in legume cells.

works.title: Correction: Rubisco dark inhibition in angiosperms shows a complex distribution pattern
An EjSPT–EjTCP4– EjRR8 regulatory module links cytokinin homeostasis and cell proliferation to fruit growth in loquat
works.abstract: Fruit size is a key determinant of crop yield and commercial value. Here, we investigated fruit development in two loquat cultivars with contrasting fruit sizes. Through hormone quantification, cytological analyses, and transcriptome profiling, we found that cytokinin-related changes were closely associated with loquat fruit-size variation, and further identified EjRR8 as a key regulatory gene. Gain- and loss-of-function analyses indicated that EjRR8 modulates cytokinin accumulation and cell proliferation, thereby contributing to fruit growth. Furthermore, we identified EjSPT and EjTCP4 as upstream transcription factors of EjRR8. Yeast one-hybrid, Dual-Luciferase, and EMSA assays showed that both factors directly bind to the EjRR8 promoter, while functional validation demonstrated that they positively affect cytokinin accumulation. Notably, EjSPT and EjTCP4 physically interacted and synergistically activated EjRR8 expression, forming a regulatory module that links transcriptional control with cytokinin-related responses and cell proliferation. These findings reveal an EjSPT-EjTCP4-EjRR8 module associated with cytokinin accumulation, cell division and fruit-size variation. This study provides a molecular framework for breeding loquat cultivars with larger fruits and offers broader insights into the regulation of fruit development in woody crops.

works.title: Dynamic regulatory control of plant heteromeric ACCase revealed by spatiotemporal stoichiometry
works.abstract: Despite being comprised of four catalytic subunits and affected by three classes of regulatory proteins, the plastid heteromeric acetyl-CoA carboxylase (hetACCase) remains poorly understood from both structural and protein stoichiometry perspectives. Here, we expanded an AQUA-multiple reaction monitoring (AQUA-MRM) assay to quantify the absolute abundance of hetACCase catalytic subunits and regulatory effectors across Arabidopsis organs, developmental stages, and light conditions. Our results demonstrate that the in vivo stoichiometry of ACCase catalytic subunits and regulatory effectors varies with organ, light, and development. The catalytic subunits to ACCase were detected in all organs under all conditions, unlike most heterotrophs which often only conditionally express ACCase. The β-CT subunit accumulated at higher quantities than its three catalytic counterparts, possibly because it is plastid encoded. Highest average abundance of β-CT was observed in 11 DAF developing seed (112 fmol/µg), followed by young leaves (54.7 fmol/µg), 7 DAF pod walls (17.1 fmol/µg), and roots (16.8 fmol/µg). Notably, catalytic subunits BC, BCCP (summed isoforms), and α-CT exhibited nearly 1:1:1 in vivo stoichiometry throughout the plant. Maximum average abundances of BC, BCCP, and α-CT were 95.1, 63.4, and 79.6 fmol/µg in developing seeds, 34.0, 26.5, and 29.1 fmol/µg in leaves, 12.1, 8.6, and 8.4 fmol/µg in pod walls, and 8.5, 6.0, and 6.4 fmol/µg in roots, respectively, indicating structural homogeneity and coordinated expression. In contrast, regulatory effectors, BADC, CTI, and PII did not obey any consistent stoichiometric relationship with catalytic subunits, often exceeding them in abundance, but in unique and specific ways suggesting adaptive roles for each effector class to sense and regulate a ubiquitously-expressed plant ACCase. Highest levels of both PII and BADC were observed in developing seed and pod walls, with PII peaking at 15 DAF seed (550 fmol/µg) and BADC (summed isoforms) reaching 239 fmol/µg at 11 DAF. In pod walls, BADC (42.5 fmol/µg) exceeded PII (27.6 fmol/µg) at 7 DAF. In leaves, BADC (119 fmol/µg in young leaves) and CTI (98.5 fmol/µg in mature leaves) were predominant, whereas roots were characterized primarily by BADC accumulation (34.8 fmol/µg). Increases observed after light onset in hetACCase catalytic subunits and regulatory effectors were most pronounced in leaves, followed by pod walls, and developing seeds, whereas roots displayed weak or inverse responses. Together, these findings redefine plastid hetACCase as a dynamic metabolic hub that integrates developmental, metabolic, and environmental signals through tissue-specific regulatory modules, including PII, CTIs, and BADCs, to coordinate fatty acid biosynthetic flux; a strategy that attenuates activity in response to cellular cues.

works.title: Proteases and proteolysis in biomolecular condensates
works.abstract: Proteases have long been conceptualised as enzymes operating in dilute aqueous environments. Yet many localise to biomolecular condensates, which arise through phase separation. We argue that protease behaviour is governed by the condensate's physical regime: a dynamic liquid-like state, a surface-associated wetting layer, a slowed gel-like state, or a kinetically arrested solid. Each regime constrains protease kinetics, for example by slowing diffusion of protease and substrate. Activity can also be dictated by condensate composition rather than protease concentration alone: the local environment can alter substrate affinities, reshape enzyme conformational equilibria beyond bulk mass-action predictions, and buffer pH. Proteolysis need not occur in the dense phase; the interface can be an additional reaction compartment. Recent evidence suggests that condensates can hydrolyse substrates even without an enzyme, so cleavage attributed to a resident protease needs a catalytically inactive control to separate enzyme-catalysed proteolysis from condensate-mediated hydrolysis. Examining plant proteases through these lenses, we argue that the regimes themselves can be a consequence of proteolysis. Direct evidence linking proteases to condensate regulation, and vice versa, remains limited. Closing this gap will require regime-aware kinetics, phase-resolved measurements of dense-phase concentration, mobility and turnover, and falsifiable models integrating proteolysis with condensate physics.

works.title: Supraoptimal Mycorrhizal Colonisation Elicits Defence and Depletes Rhizosphere Inhabiting Massilia in Mild Salt‑Stressed Maize: A Split‑Root Comparison of Locally Colonised Roots
works.abstract: Environmental conditions, such as light availability, affect the growth‑promoting effects of arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) symbiosis. However, how the root‑rhizosphere continuum responds when mycorrhizal structures become unsuitable due to environmental deterioration remains unresolved. Using a split‑root system under mild salinity and low light, we generated two AM colonisation states (moderate and supraoptimal) and focused on roots with similar colonisation rates to compare local responses under different whole‑plant symbiotic backgrounds. Supraoptimal colonisation reduced the mycorrhizal growth response compared with moderate colonisation, and this reduction was uncoupled from ion homoeostasis. Root transcriptomics and rhizosphere exudates revealed that supraoptimal colonisation induced jasmonate/ethylene‑mediated defence responses, downregulated carbon transporter genes, and shifted exudation from symbiosis‑supporting lipids/terpenoids toward defence‑related amino acid derivatives. Consequently, supraoptimal colonisation reduced beneficial bacteria, notably Massilia, and simplified co‑occurrence networks. We propose a model in which salt stress and low light drive a host‑mediated "defence‑symbiosis" trade‑off, reducing the mycorrhizal growth response under supraoptimal AM colonisation. These findings provide a mechanistic framework for optimising AM applications in saline systems.

works.title: BvCaM7 Participates in Sugar Beet ( Beta vulgaris L.) Resistance to CLS (Cercospora Leaf Spot) by Activating BvPAL via BvMYB108 and Is Accompanied by Calcium Dynamics
works.abstract: CLS (Cercospora leaf spot) is a major constraint in sugar beet (Beta vulgaris L.) cultivation, yet the functions of CaM/CML family members in CLS resistance are unclear. This study identified the CaM/CML family in sugar beet and focused on BvCaM7, which was significantly upregulated under CLS. Calcium measurements revealed differential calcium dynamics between resistant and susceptible varieties at late stages. Lignin staining revealed enhanced vascular lignification in resistant lines. Molecular interaction assays confirmed that BvCaM7 interacts with BvCNGC14 and BvMYB108. LUC assays confirmed that BvMYB108 activates the PAL promoter, and coexpression with BvCaM7 enhanced this effect. Transient overexpression of BvCaM7 or BvMYB108 in tobacco was associated with reduced lesion development following Cercospora beticola (C. beticola.) inoculation, although defence gene induction kinetics (PR2/3/4, PAL, COL, PDF1.2) differed: BvMYB108 peaked at 12 h, whereas BvCaM7 sustained expression until 24 h. Both overexpressions increased superoxide dismutase (SOD) and peroxidase (POD) activities, but decreased catalase (CAT) activity. In summary, BvCaM7 activates the PAL pathway via BvMYB108, enhancing lignin-related defence. Furthermore, the BvCaM7-BvCNGC14 interaction and concomitant calcium changes provide clues for the potential involvement of calcium signalling. However, its specific role requires further validation. This study provides candidate genes for breeding CLS-resistant sugar beet.

works.title: Transcriptomic responses of sugarcane to drought stress are modulated by bacterial synthetic communities
works.abstract: Abstract Drought intensification due to climate change poses a significant constraint on global sugarcane security, as sugarcane requires substantial water for optimal growth. While Synthetic Communities (SynComs) offer potential to improve drought resilience, their application and mechanisms of action remain murky, particularly in sugarcane. Here, we used transcriptomics analysis to examine how SynComs may modulate responses to drought stress in sugarcane. We examined five potential SynComs (SC) and selected SC3, a promising consortium, for detailed gene expression analysis. This selection was based on the excellent performance of SC3-inoculated plants, as indicated by higher plant height, P uptake, and osmoprotectant content compared to other SynComs and control (C) plants. Transcriptomic analysis revealed differences in signal transduction: in SC3-inoculated plants, MAPK signaling was prominent, whereas in C plants, signaling relied more on plant hormones. Moreover, differences in energy allocation and secondary metabolite production as defense responses to drought stress were observed. SC3-inoculated plants appear to allocate energy to maintaining lipid membrane integrity and lignification, while C plants focus on antioxidant activity via flavonoids. The results indicate that bacterial SynComs inoculants can modulate drought stress responses. Overall, our study suggests that SynComs offer sustainable solutions to drought challenges in agriculture.

works.title: Metabolomic profiling unveils differential modulation of tomato fruit quality by microbial interventions
Root saprotropism: A tropism guided by environmental pH sensing
works.abstract: In saprotropism, roots perceive fungal-derived acidic pH gradients via the RGF-RGFR module to trigger asymmetric abscisic acid signaling, reorient microtubules, and drive root bending away from decay. Extracellular pH is a key convergence mode that mediates diverse plant-microbe interactions.

works.title: CSN5A and DEG1 Contribute to FT Stability in Temperature-Dependent Flowering
works.abstract: FLOWERING LOCUS T (FT) functions as a florigen and plays a central role in the floral transition. Although FT regulation has been extensively characterized at the transcriptional level, mechanisms controlling FT protein stability remain poorly understood. Here, we provide evidence for a temperature-responsive proteolytic process involving COP9 signalosome subunit 5A (CSN5A) and the serine protease DEGRADATION OF PERIPLASMIC PROTEINS 1 (DEG1) that contributes to flowering-time regulation. csn5a mutants flower early at low ambient temperature and exhibit increased accumulation of a myc-tagged FT protein, suggesting post-translational regulation. deg1 mutants also flower early under low-temperature conditions, and genetic analyses reveal additive flowering phenotypes in csn5a deg1 double mutants, supporting partially independent contributions of CSN5A and DEG1. Biochemical assays show that recombinant DEG1 promotes FT degradation in vitro, whereas serine protease inhibition attenuates FT turnover in vivo. Phloem-specific expression of CSN5A restores the flowering phenotype of csn5a mutants, consistent with a vascular domain of action relevant to FT biology. Together, these findings reveal a temperature-responsive post-translational layer of FT regulation that contributes to flowering-time control.

works.title: Promoter variation in BraHDAC1 modulates stomatal regulation and thermotolerance in Brassica rapa
works.abstract: Heat stress severely limits the productivity of Brassica rapa, a key vegetable crop worldwide. Deciphering the genetic basis of thermotolerance is essential for developing climate-resilient cultivars. By integrating genome-wide association studies (GWAS) with bulked segregant analysis (BSA), we identified 2 single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP1 and SNP2) in the promoter of the histone deacetylase gene BraHDAC1, which underlies natural variation in heat tolerance. These SNPs create a functional ABRE-CE cis-regulatory module exclusively in thermotolerant haplotypes (Hap1 and Hap3), enabling heat-induced transcription via binding of the transcription factor BraAREB1. Enhanced BraHDAC1 activity in turn represses the pectin methylesterase (PME) gene BraPME1 through histone H3K9/K14 deacetylation at its promoter. This repression, together with the coordinated regulation of additional PME and pectin methylesterase inhibitors (PMEI) genes, is associated with altered total PME activity and broader changes in pectin methylesterification, which may contribute to temporal stomatal regulation. This regulation involves early stomatal opening and increased transpiration associated with lower leaf temperature, consistent with enhanced transpirational cooling, followed by later closure to conserve water. Our findings define a BraAREB1-BraHDAC1 regulatory module in which BraPME1 is one functionally validated downstream target, illustrating how a cis-regulatory variation coordinates transcriptional, epigenetic, and cell wall modification responses to heat stress. The SNP and its associated regulatory module provide direct targets for marker-assisted breeding and genetic improvement of thermotolerant B. rapa.

works.title: Maize endonuclease NOB1 couples ribosome biogenesis with translational regulation during kernel development
works.abstract: NOB1-mediated cleavage of 20S pre-rRNA represents a critical quality-control step during cytoplasmic maturation of the eukaryotic 40S ribosomal subunit, yet its developmental significance in crops remains largely unexplored. Here, we identified two highly conserved maize NOB1 paralogs, ZmNOB1a and ZmNOB1b, both exhibiting RNA-binding and endonuclease activities and associating with pre-40S ribosomal particles. Genetic analyses demonstrated that the two paralogs function redundantly, but with unequal contributions, to support gametophyte viability and kernel development. Simultaneous disruption of ZmNOB1 activity resulted in severely impaired male gametophyte transmission, markeldly reduced female gamete viability, and profound defects in embryo and endosperm development. Molecular analyses further revealed widespread disruption of pre-rRNA maturation, including defective D-site cleavage, accompanied by impaired ribosome assembly and reduced translational capacity. Consistent with these molecular defects, mutant kernels exhibited decreased starch and storage protein accumulation, together with elevated levels of free ribosomal subunits and reduced 80S monosomes and polysomes. Moreover, ZmNOB1 exhibited co-sedimentation and directly interacted with the translation initiation factor eIF4A, implying a potential functional coordination between late ribosome maturation and translation initiation. Collectively, our findings establish ZmNOB1-mediated pre-rRNA processing as a key determinant of translational competence, reproductive fitness, and seed filling in maize.

works.title: The Plant Ubiquitin System: From Identification of E2 and E3 enzymes to Molecular Mechanisms and Biological Function
works.abstract: Ubiquitination is an essential post-translation modification involved in almost every cellular process and is critical for proper functioning of eukaryotic cells. The modification involves the covalent attachment of ubiquitin, a small, conserved peptide, to select proteins. One or more ubiquitin molecules may be attached in varying configurations, leading to a range of possible outcomes that regulate protein function, including changes in location, stability, and activity. Components of the ubiquitin system are highly expanded in plants relative to other eukaryotes and play major roles in almost all aspects of plant growth and development, from phytohormone perception and signalling, to maintaining nutrient homeostasis in the face of fluctuating environmental conditions. We begin this Centennial Review by highlighting two Plant Physiology papers that contributed to the identification and characterisation of ubiquitin enzymes. We then provide an update on our understanding of how plants use the ubiquitin system to link environmental change with plant growth and development. We first focus on recent advances in understanding how the structure and function of ubiquitin ligases are modulated by phytohormones and nutrient status. We then highlight emerging knowledge linking components of the ubiquitin system with biomolecular condensates, including stress granules, and discuss the potential functional implications.

works.title: Class III chitinases in Medicago truncatula facilitate arbuscular mycorrhizal symbiosis with Rhizophagus intraradices
works.abstract: Plant chitinases are important defense enzymes in plant-microbe interactions and also participate in nodule symbiosis between legumes and nitrogen-fixing rhizobia. However, the roles of chitinases in arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) symbiosis remain incompletely defined. In this study, we characterized 2 class III chitinase genes in the legume Medicago truncatula (ecotype R108), namely MtCHIT3e and MtCHIT3f. Heterologous expression in Nicotiana benthamiana confirmed hydrolytic activity toward colloidal chitin, a fluorogenic chitooligosaccharide substrate, chitooligosaccharides, and lipo-chitooligosaccharides. In M. truncatula roots inoculated with AM fungi, transcripts of the 2 genes were significantly upregulated. Analysis of M. truncatula hairy roots transformed with promoter-β-glucuronidase constructs indicated strong induction of MtCHIT3e and MtCHIT3f promoter activity in response to applied chitooligosaccharide and lipo-chitooligosaccharide signals. Furthermore, fluorescent protein fusions localized the chitinases predominantly to the apoplast of host cells during AM colonization. Tnt1 insertion mutants in the chitinase genes exhibited reduced AM colonization, whereas nodule formation induced by Sinorhizobium meliloti was unaffected. Together, these results support a role for class III chitinases in promoting AM symbiosis and provide genetic evidence that they are required for optimal root colonization by AM fungi.

works.title: Multi-omics profiling reveals common and specific molecular responses to butenolide perception
works.abstract: Strigolactones (SLs) and Karrikins (KARs) are butenolide compounds that have been characterized to act like phytohormones. While SLs are synthesized endogenously in plants from carotenoids, KARs are a known constituent of wildfire smoke emanating from the combustion of carbohydrates in burning plant tissues. Despite their different sources of origin, they have similar chemical structures and are perceived through similar receptor complexes. However, the compound-specific molecular pathways downstream of these two signalling molecules remains to be elucidated. Hereby, we adopt an integrated approach combining transcriptome, proteome, proteogenome and metabolome profiling to compare the molecular responses of seeds and seedlings to the synthetic strigolactone analog, rac-GR24 and to the karrikinolide, KAR1 in Arabidopsis seeds or seedlings. This multi-omics approach allowed us to delineate the key conserved, and compound-specific, regulators such as transcription factors, splicing-related proteins, and primary metabolites that could play important functional roles in establishing the signaling response to these butenolides. Correlational analysis suggested differential splicing and metabolite regulation in response to rac-GR24 and KARs suggesting potential molecular targets including the TCA cycle. Treatment of mutants of key enzymes of energy metabolism, identified in the above studies, revealed that these mutants showed altered metabolic responses to butenolide treatment. In summary, our integrative dataset reveals strong associations between butenolide treatment and TCA cycle related changes across multiple molecular levels, and provides a foundation for generating testable hypotheses on how these signals interface with energy metabolism.

works.title: Trichoderma elicitor CP3 induces phosphorylation and nuclear export of SRP to enhance tomato resistance to gray mold
works.abstract: Beneficial Trichoderma fungi enhance plant immunity, but the molecular mechanisms of elicitor-mediated immune priming are still not well defined. Here, we identified a cerato-platanin (CP) family elicitor, CP3, from T. asperellum that enhances tomato resistance to Botrytis cinerea. CP3 is secreted and localizes to the host nucleus, where it interacts with the tomato protein SRP. This interaction recruits casein kinase 1 to phosphorylate SRP at Ser-185, thereby triggering its nuclear export to the plasma membrane. Subsequently, SRP binds the ubiquinone biosynthesis protein COQ9, forming a signaling module that activates reactive oxygen species production and jasmonate/ethylene defense pathways to establish induced systemic resistance. Genetic disruption of CP3, SRP, or COQ9 abolishes CP3-induced resistance, confirming their essential roles. Our findings reveal a complete CP3-SRP-COQ9 signaling axis through which a beneficial fungal elicitor reprograms host nucleocytoplasmic trafficking to activate tailored immunity, offering new molecular targets for engineering disease-resistant crops.

works.title: The CsBLH9-CsOVATE module regulates heat tolerance via chlorophyll degradation in cucumber
works.abstract: Heat stress has become a primary environmental factor that severely threatens crop yield and quality. Despite many genes having been identified to participate in heat response, natural alleles of heat response genes that can be utilized in crop breeding are scarce, and the underlying mechanisms remain enigmatic. In this study, we identified a BEL1-like Homeodomain (BLH) transcription factor CsBLH9, through genome-wide association study (GWAS), and demonstrated its positive role in heat response. The natural variants of CsBLH9 exhibit different levels of heat tolerance and differential response to gibberellin (GA) treatment. Knockout of CsBLH9 resulted in sensitive heat response and reduced chlorophyll levels. CsBLH9 can directly bind to the promoters of chlorophyll catabolic genes stay-green (CsSGR) and pheophorbide a oxygenase (CsPAO) to inhibit their expression. Furthermore, we identified CsOVATE as an interacting partner of CsBLH9 that also functions as a positive regulator of heat tolerance. Csovate mutants showed phenotypes similar to Csblh9 mutants under heat stress, and CsOVATE enhanced the CsBLH9-mediated inhibition of CsSGR and CsPAO expression. Therefore, our findings suggested that CsBLH9-CsOVATE acts as a module that regulates heat tolerance via chlorophyll degradation in cucumber, and the natural alleles of CsBLH9 provide new targets for crop improvement under heat stress.

works.title: Legacy effects of selective coppicing on forest regeneration in Bronze Age Italy
works.abstract: Unambiguous evidence of sophisticated woodland and land-use management in Bronze Age southern Europe is presented from the Terramare culture in northern Italy. Archaeological layers dated to ~3,600 years ago reveal a society whose economy was structurally dependent on wood, used as both building material and fuel, defining what we term here a 'Wood Age' culture. High-resolution pollen sequences and stratigraphic data from key sites indicate that oak-dominated woodlands regenerated through long-term recurrent cycles of selective coppicing targeting specific broad-leaved trees (Quercus species, Carpinus betulus, Corylus avellana and Ostrya carpinifolia) and that these practices followed repeated cycles of cutting and regrowth under sustained human disturbance. The Terramare economy relied on a multifunctional agro-silvopastoral system integrating woodland management, crop rotation, animal husbandry and water control. Yet, selected woodland patches were maintained for fruit gathering and boundary marking, highlighting a conscious balance between exploitation and ecological awareness. This land-use strategy sustained the Terramare communities for centuries but also drove profound and partly irreversible transformations of soils and water systems, at times exceeding local sustainability thresholds. By revealing long-term, regeneration-driven forest management, our results challenge the assumption that many temperate lowland forests represent natural baselines, highlighting instead the deep ecological legacies of past human intervention.

works.title: Pollen records reveal the lasting ecological legacy of Bronze Age cyclical woodland management
Improved temperature and photoperiod response functions to better link genotype to phenotype prediction for soybean phenology
works.abstract: Gene-to-phenotype modeling requires robust mechanistic frameworks, yet widely used soybean phenology models rely on older datasets with limited genotypic representation and do not explicitly account for twilight effects. We quantified soybean phenology responses to temperature (11-35 °C) and photoperiod (12-16 h) using 20 modern cultivars spanning maturity groups (MG) 0-7, evaluated across 12 controlled-environment experiments and 13 field experiments in the USA. Our objectives were to (1) reconstruct temperature and photoperiod response functions for three developmental phases (emergence - flowering, flowering - beginning seed filling, and beginning seed filling - physiological maturity), (2) determine whether these responses vary among cultivars, and (3) identify the twilight value that maximizes prediction accuracy and evaluate an improved soybean phenology module. Temperature responses were best described by a curvilinear function, with optimum temperature declining from vegetative to reproductive development (30.4 to 22.1 °C). Photoperiod responses followed a bilinear model, with photoperiod sensitivity and minimum phase duration varying systematically with maturity group, whereas no photoperiod response was detected during the seed filling period. Prediction accuracy across independent field experiments was maximized using a twilight angle of -6°, with an uncalibrated multiplicative model achieving a root mean squared error (RMSE) <10 days and an index of agreement (d-index) >0.96. Our results show that variation in photoperiod response is driven primarily by photoperiod sensitivity rather than the critical photoperiod threshold, improving cultivar parameterization, reducing equifinality, and providing a stronger physiological foundation for improving crop model prediction accuracy across diverse genotypes and environments.

works.title: A BmMYB14 – UGT Regulatory Module Contributes to Dammarane-Type Triterpene Biosynthesis in Bacopa monnieri
works.abstract: Bacosides, a key glycosylated dammarane-type triterpenes of Bacopa monnieri, exhibit diverse pharmacological activities, yet the enzymatic and regulatory mechanisms governing their biosynthesis remain underexplored. In this study, we functionally characterized the methyl jasmonate-inducible glycosyltransferase UGT94AV1 and demonstrated its ability to glycosylate diverse triterpenoid substrates, with the highest catalytic efficiency observed for ginsenoside RH2. Recombinant UGT94AV1 demonstrated a capacity for sequential glycosylation by efficiently catalyzing the transfer of a glucose moiety to the aglycone core, i.e., jujubogenin and pseudojujubogenin, derived from the periodate oxidation of bacoside A, and its corresponding monoglycosides. Overexpression of UGT94AV1 in B. monnieri enhanced the accumulation of jujubogenin-derived bacosides, while its knockdown reduced their levels. Further, transcriptome analysis has identified BmMYB14 co-expressing with UGT94AV1 and the previously characterized UGT79A18. Overexpression of BmMYB14 significantly upregulated UGT79A18 and UGT94AV1, whereas silencing of BmMYB14 markedly reduced their transcript levels. The expressions of UGT94AV1 and UGT79A18 in BmMYB14 OE and KD lines were consistent with enhanced accumulation of bacosides in OE lines and reduced in KD lines. Yeast one-hybrid and dual-luciferase assays using the promoter regions of UGT94AV1 and UGT79A18 further demonstrate that BmMYB14 transcriptionally regulates UGT79A18 and UGT94AV1, and hence contributes to the dammarane-type triterpene biosynthesis in Bacopa monnieri.

works.title: Nitrate metabolism and regulation of legume nitrogen fixation
works.abstract: The interaction between nitrate and symbiotic nitrogen fixation is complex, diverse, and tightly regulated at multiple levels. The effects of nitrate are strongly dependent on the specific legume-rhizobia symbiosis and on the concentration and exposure time to nitrate. This has hampered studies on nitrate inhibition of nodule development and function. Here, we critically review most of the proposed mechanisms, which include carbohydrate deprivation, inactivation of nitrogenase and/or leghemoglobin by nitrite and/or nitric oxide, feedback regulation of nodule activity by an increase of nitrogenous metabolites in the phloem, and oxygen limitation through an oxygen diffusion barrier (ODB) mainly located in the inner cortex. Several hypotheses to explain the limitation of oxygen access to the nitrogen-fixing zone include glycoprotein occlusion of intercellular spaces, shifts in K+ and H2O2, and enhanced 'protective' respiration and activity of the ascorbate-associated enzymes in the cortical cells. Important progress has been made with the identification of nitrate transporters (NPF and NRT2 families) and transcription factors involved in nitrate regulation of nodulation (NIN, NLPs, and FUN) and in nitrate-induced nodule senescence (NAC094 and SNAP1/2/3/4). However, with the exception of a genetic study showing that suberin deposition in the endodermis is involved in nodule oxygen permeability, the molecular mechanisms underlying the ODB remain a mystery.

works.title: Integrating arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi in Mediterranean Climate-Smart Viticulture: Progress, bottlenecks, and future directions
works.abstract: Climate change is increasingly threatening global viticulture through rising temperatures, changing rainfall patterns, and extreme weather events, affecting grapevine physiology, yield, composition and vineyard health and, ultimately, leading to changes in wine composition and typicity. Particular attention is being paid to arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF), soil microorganisms that form symbiotic associations with grapevine roots. They are able to improve water and nutrient uptake and plant tolerance to environmental stressors. This review summarizes the current knowledge on the impact of climate change on grapevine performance, focusing on Mediterranean viticulture, as well as the range of potential short- and long-term adaptation strategies to reduce its effects. Among them, this review explores integrating AMF into climate-smart viticulture and describes their potential to enhance grapevine resilience to environmental stresses. The review discusses how climate change may influence native mycorrhizal communities in vineyard soils and when commercial AMF inoculants may be necessary to apply. Additionally, it addresses the opportunities and limitations associated with their use. Overall, the available evidence suggests that AMF are a promising component of sustainable vineyard management and may improve vineyard resilience under future climate scenarios. However, more research is needed to optimize their application and understand their long-term effects on different viticultural systems.

works.title: Integrating environmental adaptation, breeding, and rhizobia bioinoculants for soybean expansion in Europe
works.abstract: Europe's heavy dependence on imported protein is environmentally and strategically costly. Soybean (Glycine max) offers a great opportunity to close this gap. Soybean cultivation can reduce reliance on synthetic nitrogen (N) fertiliser through its symbiosis with N-fixing bacteria (rhizobia). Nevertheless, it remains a relatively new crop across much of Europe and establishing it in the continent's diverse environments raises challenges of climate adaptation, symbiotic N fixation, and crop management. We argue that these challenges must be addressed together rather than separately, because yield stability, N fixation, and environmental stress resilience emerge from the interactions between plant genotype, rhizobial strain, environment, and soil and crop management practices. Drawing on lessons from major soybean-producing regions, we review environmental adaptation through maturity-group selection and stress-resilience breeding, rhizobia inoculant design, and the management practices that shape symbiotic and crop performance. We further examine genetic, genomic, and computational resources that make these interactions predictable and optimisable and identify priorities for future research and practice.

works.title: Induced Volatile Chemistry and Arthropod Predation Across a Tree Diversity Gradient
works.abstract: Plant volatile organic compounds (VOCs) play a key role in defence against herbivores and in mediating multitrophic interactions. Yet, how surrounding plant diversity modulates these responses in forest trees remains poorly understood. We examined the effects of tree species richness on induced VOC emissions and arthropod predation in Quercus petraea in a biodiversity-ecosystem functioning experiment. Individual branches were repeatedly induced with methyl jasmonate and paired with non-induced controls within the same tree. VOCs were collected using PDMS tubes after the first and last induction rounds and analyzed by TD-GC-MS. Predation was quantified using plasticine caterpillars. Jasmonate induction strongly altered VOC profiles and effects increased after repeated treatments. Tree species richness modulated VOC composition during the first sampling period, particularly affecting sesquiterpenes. Compound-specific analyses revealed that β-Ocimene was negatively associated with predation probability during the second sampling period. However, absolute VOC class emissions did not explain variation in arthropod predation probability, while compound class-level composition showed only weak and inconsistent effects across sampling periods. These results suggest that indirect defence outcomes in terms of predator responses are unlikely to depend on VOC class-level emission strength or broad VOC class composition but may instead be mediated by fine-scale properties of volatile blends.

works.title: A Citrus Mosaic Virus‐Based Vector for Virus‐Induced Gene Silencing in Tobacco and Citrus
works.abstract: Summary statement Virus‐induced gene silencing (VIGS) has emerged as a powerful tool for the rapid and efficient functional analysis of plant genes. However, the lack of efficient and rapid reverse genetics tools specifically tailored for citrus, coupled with the limited applicability of existing VIGS vectors in this genus. This research presents a robust set of VIGS vectors suitable for both tobacco and citrus, offering a valuable tool for functional genomics research.

works.title: DDM1 Shapes Transgenerational Epigenetic Inheritance of Diverse Chromatin States
works.abstract: Transgenerational epigenetic inheritance (TEI) enables plants to transmit adaptive chromatin states across generations. However, the mechanisms by which these states are maintained and stabilised during TEI remain unclear. Here, we investigate the TEI of repressive marks (H3K27me3 and DNA methylation) together with the active mark H3K4me3, which are associated with distinct reinforcement mechanisms, using reciprocal crosses of Arabidopsis ecotypes Col-0 and C24. We show that all three marks undergo TEI but exhibit distinct inheritance patterns depending on their reinforcement mechanisms. These inheritance patterns are modulated by DDM1, which coordinates the propagation of repressive chromatin states. Our results indicate that chromatin remodelling, through its effects on nucleosome organisation and histone variant dynamics, plays a key role in shaping TEI via chromatin context in plants.

works.title: Stem rust resistance in North American spring wheat to Ug99 and other virulent pathotypes of Puccinia graminis f. sp. tritici
works.abstract: KEY MESSAGE: North American spring wheat shows limited seedling resistance to a diverse set of exotic Pgt races but harbors valuable field resistance, including a strong locus for field resistance on chromosome 7AL. The emergence and spread of Ug99 and other races of Puccinia graminis f. sp. tritici (Pgt) with virulence to widely deployed resistance genes threaten global wheat production. This study evaluated North American spring wheat germplasm for seedling responses to four Pgt races (TTKSK, TTKSF+, TKTTF, and TRTTF) and for field response across five environments in Ethiopia and Kenya. Seedling evaluation revealed significant race-specific variation, with 82% of the lines exhibiting resistance to race TKTTF but very limited resistance to the other races. Gene postulation based on resistance patterns suggested a high frequency of Sr7a (~ 92%) in this panel, with only a few lines (~ 5%) carrying Sr8a, Sr11, and/or Sr31. Field evaluations in Ethiopia and Kenya demonstrated quantitative variation for field response, with several lines showing consistent field resistance. Association mapping identified 37 significant associations for seedling resistance, representing 17 unique genomic regions. For field response, 15 significant associations were detected, including a region on chromosome arm 7AL that was consistently detected across environments. Further analysis indicated that this locus confers adult-plant resistance (APR) and might be independent of known stem rust resistance genes located in the region. Hence, KASP assay was developed to enable marker-assisted selection and further investigation of this locus. This study highlights limited seedling resistance but identifies promising sources of field resistance against exotic Pgt races and provides valuable insights into the genetics underlying both seedling and field responses in North American germplasm.

works.title: PDS5A restricts SYN4-dependent long-range chromatin contacts to shape TAD-like chromatin architecture in Arabidopsis
works.abstract: Abstract Three-dimensional genome folding in vertebrates, such as the formation of topologically associating domains (TADs), depends on cohesin-mediated loop extrusion, yet its regulation in plants remains unresolved. Using Hi–C and Micro-C, we show that Arabidopsis cohesin regulator PDS5A is a key modulator of chromatin loop extrusion and TAD-like architecture. The TAD-like domain patterns in pds5a are highly similar across tissues and ploidy levels. Genetic evidence reveals that TAD-like domains require the plant kleisin SYN4 and are opposed by WAPL1/2, with PDS5A serving as the major cohesin-unloading factor. Biochemical assays show that PDS5A associates with cohesin independently of its Tudor domain-mediated H3K4me1 binding. Micro-C further identifies accessible, highly transcribed promoters as chromatin loop and stripe anchors. Finally, mutational disruption of distal chromatin anchors shows that newly formed chromatin contacts in pds5a can act as cis-regulatory modules that influence target gene expression. Together, these findings identify a PDS5A-regulated chromatin extrusion module that contributes to plant 3D genome organization and uncover a promoter-based logic for loop anchoring and transcriptional control in plants.

works.title: Breaking the ice: uncovering miPEP171b control of grapevine cold stress response
ACR11 promotes nitrogen assimilation and protein productivity during urea cultivation in duckweed Lemna minor
works.abstract: Nitrogen assimilation plays a crucial role in plant growth and protein accumulation. Urea is a widely used and low-cost nitrogen source; therefore, efficient assimilation of urea-derived nitrogen is critical for biomass accumulation and protein production in plants. However, the regulatory factors that enhance this process remain poorly understood. Here, we identify the chloroplast-localized ACT DOMAIN REPEAT 11 (ACR11) as a positive regulator of nitrogen assimilation in duckweed. Overexpression (OE) of LpACR11 increased growth rate, protein content and protein productivity of duckweed Lemna minor ZH0403 under urea nutrition, whereas RNAi-mediated knockdown caused opposite effects. Heterologous expression of LpACR11 in tobacco and rice also enhanced biomass and protein accumulation under urea cultivation conditions. Biochemical and metabolic analyses showed that LpACR11 OE was associated with increased Fd-GOGAT (ferredoxin-dependent glutamate synthase) activity, elevated glutamate accumulation, reduced ammonium accumulation and increased total amino acid content. Glutamate treatment further promoted GS2 (plastid glutamine synthetase) expression and activity, supporting a working model in which ACR11-associated enhancement of Fd-GOGAT activity increases glutamate accumulation and thereby promotes GS2-associated nitrogen assimilation. Together, these results indicate that ACR11 enhances chloroplast nitrogen-assimilation capacity and protein productivity during urea cultivation, providing a potential genetic target for improving protein productivity in duckweed and other crops.

works.title: Fern phloem evolution records a trend of decreasing conductivity through geological time
works.abstract: Phloem, the sugar-transporting tissue in vascular plants, is one of the most important but least characterized tissues from an evolutionary perspective. Here we substantially extend the evidence for phloem evolution by carrying out a histological investigation of phloem conducting cells, termed sieve elements, in 26 extant fern species spanning 21 families and making over 18,000 measurements. We report high diversity in fern phloem and that sieve element radius preserves a strong phylogenetic signal. We also detect clear scaling relationships between sieve element radius and both leaf and vasculature characteristics in the leptosporangiate ferns. By integrating fossils into our analysis, we recognized a trend of decreasing sieve element radius and total conducting area through geological time. We conclude that this decrease likely had a major functional impact by reducing phloem conductivity in the highly diverse polypod ferns that diversified into angiosperm-dominated ecosystems.

works.title: Pantoea ananatis- triggered systemic resistance requires root sensing through the LORE receptor kinase in Arabidopsis
works.abstract: Systemic immunity induced by beneficial bacteria enhances plant resilience to subsequent pathogen attacks. However, the mechanisms by which plants perceive these bacteria and translate this perception into a systemic response remain poorly understood. The Brassicaceae LIPOOLIGOSACCHARIDE-SPECIFIC REDUCED ELICITATION (LORE) receptor kinase is the direct sensor of bacterial medium-chain-length 3-hydroxy fatty acids (mc-3-OH-FAs) and 3-(3-hydroxyalkanoyloxy)alkanoic acids (HAAs), both of which activate local Brassicaceae immunity. Here, we show that the HAA-producing bacterium Pantoea ananatis BRT175 can colonize Arabidopsis thaliana roots independently of the production of HAAs, but these compounds induce a lore-dependent local immune response in roots. P. ananatis triggers induced systemic resistance (ISR) against the necrotrophic fungus Botrytis cinerea, but not against the hemibiotrophic bacterium Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato DC3000. This ISR can be mimicked by HAAs or 3-hydroxy-decanoic acid (3-OH-C10), the strongest agonist of LORE. Both bacterium- and 3-hydroxylated fatty acid MAMP-induced ISR against B. cinerea rely on LORE-mediated sensing, involve salicylic acid, jasmonic acid/ethylene signaling pathways, and activate similar defense gene expression profiles in infected leaves. Our results demonstrate that lipidic microbe-associated molecular patterns (MAMPs) produced by beneficial microorganisms are necessary and sufficient to trigger rhizobacteria-mediated ISR and could differentially activate systemic resistance against biotrophic and necrotrophic pathogens.

works.title: Root rot suppression by synthetic microbiota is associated with rhizosphere bacterial shifts and amino acid metabolism
works.abstract: Root rot caused by Fusarium oxysporum (F. oxysporum) severely constrains Codonopsis pilosula (C. pilosula) production. Indigenous culturable bacteria associated with C. pilosula were screened for antifungal activity, plant growth-promoting traits, and interstrain compatibility, and two defined three-member synthetic microbial communities, SCI and SCII, were constructed. Both SynComs alleviated root rot, with SCI showing stronger overall performance and a biocontrol efficacy of 57.8%, together with improved root growth and photosynthetic performance. Rhizosphere bacterial profiling was integrated with rhizosphere metabolite profiling and root tissue metabolomics. SynCom treatment was associated with limited changes in overall bacterial diversity but variation in specific rhizosphere taxa. In roots, pathway-enrichment patterns shifted from sulfur metabolism and oxidative stress-related processes under pathogen stress toward amino acid-related metabolism after SynCom treatment, accompanied by treatment-associated variation in medicinally relevant metabolite features. Associations between metabolic changes and potentially beneficial bacteria indicated coordinated variation between host metabolism and rhizosphere bacterial composition. In vitro assays further showed that L-valine elicited chemotactic and growth responses in a representative Sphingomonas isolate. Collectively, SynCom-mediated root rot suppression was associated with constituent-strain antagonism, plant recovery, rhizosphere bacterial shifts, and amino acid-related metabolic variation.

works.title: Defining membrane‐bound transcription factors in plant stress responses
works.abstract: fluxes, membrane fluidity, organelle redox state, and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) proteostasis, affecting nuclear gene expression. Membrane-bound transcription factors (MTFs) and related membrane-associated pathways regulate the generation, localization, and activity of nuclear-competent forms of transcription factors through proteolysis, unconventional mRNA splicing, and post-translational regulation. This mini review examines ER-to-Golgi trafficking and proteolytic activation of bZIP17/28, IRE1-dependent splicing of bZIP60/OsbZIP50, the varied activation mechanisms of NAC/NTLs, and PIP-associated MYBs. PIP-MYB studies support transporter participation in MTF activation, although the contributions of transport activity and physical interaction remain difficult to separate. Most bZIP and NAC/NTL pathways respond to changes in ER, membrane, or organelle status. We discuss their roles in proteostasis, growth restraint, and immunity, and how pathogens exploit them. We also assess the evidence for direct transporter-MTF coupling and indirect regulation by membrane state. Their use in crops will depend on establishing how endogenous MTFs are activated and switched off, and whether the resulting responses improve yield across environments.

works.title: Disruption of OsMAPKKK24 activation by the Xanthomonas oryzae effector XopY leads to compromised disease resistance in rice
works.abstract: Mitogen-activated protein (MAP) kinase (MAPK) cascades are highly conserved signaling modules that play crucial roles in plant disease resistance. Emerging evidence shows that MAPK cascades are potential targets of plant pathogen effectors. Bacterial leaf blight (BLB), caused by Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae (Xoo), is a devastating disease in rice. Xoo secretes multiple effectors into host rice plants to suppress immune activation. XopY is a conserved effector across diverse Xoo strains; however, how XopY manipulates disease resistance and what its host targets are in rice remain largely unknown. Here, we report that XopY from the Xoo strain PXO86 interacts with the MAPK kinase kinase OsMAPKKK24 and RECEPTOR-LIKE CYTOPLASMIC KINASE 55 (OsRLCK55). OsRLCK55 phosphorylates OsMAPKKK24, and both contribute to rice BLB resistance by positively regulating early immune responses. XopY suppresses the activation of OsMAPKKK24 by enhancing its intramolecular interaction between the N- and C-terminal regions. The association of XopY with OsRLCK55 and OsMAPKKK24 also interferes with their interaction and suppresses OsRLCK55-mediated transphosphorylation of OsMAPKKK24, ultimately inhibiting MAPK activation and subsequent disease resistance. Taken together, these findings not only reveal that OsRLCK55 and OsMAPKKK24 are crucial for BLB resistance but also uncover a mechanism by which XopY compromises disease resistance by manipulating OsMAPKKK24 activation in rice.

works.title: Glutathione at the Interface of Specialized Sulfur Metabolism and Sulfur Homeostasis
works.abstract: Glutathione (GSH) is a central component of plant sulfur metabolism, best known for its roles in redox homeostasis, detoxification, and stress protection. Increasing evidence indicates that GSH also functions at the interface between primary and specialized sulfur metabolism. In plants, the best-characterized examples are concentrated in a limited number of lineages, particularly Brassicaceae and Allium species, where GSH is recruited into glucosinolate, camalexin, and S-alk(en)ylcysteine sulfoxide biosynthesis. Emerging observations further highlight the contribution of GSH degradation enzymes to sulfur transfer during specialized metabolite formation, linking GSH turnover to broader sulfur allocation networks. Beyond biosynthesis, GSH conjugation plays critical roles during specialized metabolite degradation by reducing the reactivity of intermediates, shaping immune-related metabolic outcomes, and enabling sulfur recycling through coordinated pathways of GSH degradation and resynthesis. Comparable GSH-dependent strategies in microbes and animals underscore the evolutionary conservation of GSH as a versatile metabolic scaffold. Collectively, these findings support a revised view in which specialized metabolism is embedded within dynamic GSH-dependent sulfur fluxes rather than functioning as an isolated sulfur sink. This review aims to integrate recent advances that highlight the role of GSH in connecting primary and specialized sulfur metabolism in response to environmental and developmental cues.

works.title: Proximity Labeling Uncovers a Repertoire of Novel O ‐Arabinosylated Substrates for HPATs
works.abstract: Summary Statement This study delineates the HPATs interactome and O ‐arabinosylation substrates, uncovering their multi‐signal responsiveness during seed germination and expanding the network linking O ‐arabinosylation to development and stress adaptation in Arabidopsis.

works.title: Leveraging Diversity in Environmental Driven Responses Reveals a Key Role for Mesophyll Conductance and Root Sink Strength Under Elevated CO 2 and Temperature
works.abstract: ABSTRACT In future climates both CO 2 and temperature are predicted to rise. Using high‐throughput phenotyping, the diversity of 31 different banana varieties and their associated traits were leveraged to understand the impact of potential future climatic conditions of combined elevated CO 2 (e[CO 2 ]) and temperature. Under ambient CO 2 (a[CO 2 ]) the adaxial/abaxial stomatal density ratio (rSD) was identified as a strong predictor of growth, but its importance diminished when CO 2 was highly abundant. When evaluated at 400 versus 800 ppm and 30°C versus 34°C, variation in mesophyll conductance (g m ) and root sink strength drove growth under both a[CO 2 ] and e[CO 2 ]. Significant positive correlations between the e[CO 2 ] response of stomatal conductance (g s,c ), transpiration (E), root to shoot ratio, net photosynthetic rate at saturating irradiance (A sat ), maximum rate of electron transport (J max ) and maximum triose phosphate utilisation rate (TPU max ) indicated a coupling between sink strength, photosynthetic capacity and stomatal regulation. Moreover, g m and g s,c concurrently reduced under e[CO 2 ]. Interactions between acclimation towards e[CO 2 ] and temperature were evident on gas exchange and photosynthetic capacity. Under the investigated conditions, e[CO 2 ] counteracted the negative effect of the supra‐optimal temperature on growth. Varieties with high mesophyll conductance and root sink strength benefitted most from e[CO 2 ] driven growth and photosynthesis enhancement. Results were further validated in an ecotron facility. This study reveals rSD, g m and root sink strength as potential traits for crop improvement and highlights the importance of evaluating the simultaneous impact of CO 2 and temperature in future climate studies.

works.title: Identification of a stable major locus and candidate genes for drought tolerance during wheat germination
A predictive approach to genome design for multi-trait improvement and environmental adaptability via machine learning
Combining different selection criteria into breeding strategies for short-term recurrent genomic selection
works.abstract: Each breeding program must find a balance between short-term genetic gain and the preservation of genetic variation. Different selection criteria, cross selection indices and cross-planning methods have been proposed in order to improve the trade-off between both goals compared to truncation selection and mating best with best. The relative advantage of each of these measures and methods may change depending on the duration of the breeding program because each has its particular strengths and weaknesses. We specifically focused on a short-term recurrent genomic selection program spanning five generations and used two datasets with 224 oat and 293 wheat lines, respectively, for a simulation study which evaluated genetic gain and genetic diversity for 19 different breeding strategies. Overall, we found that strategies that combined different selection criteria, cross selection indices, and/or cross-planning methods rather than relying on just one measure alone resulted in a higher genetic gain compared to truncation selection while maintaining at least the same amount of genetic diversity. We therefore conclude that combining different measures into breeding strategies can enhance breeding progress without any need for additional resources.

works.title: SlNF-YC9 coordinates NF-Y trimer assembly and SlWRKY16 -mediated antagonism to regulate drought tolerance in tomato
works.abstract: Drought stress severely constrains tomato productivity, yet the transcriptional circuitry governing drought adaptation remains incompletely understood. Here, we demonstrate that SlNF-YC9 assembles with SlNF-YB3b and SlNF-YA3a into a functional NF-Y heterotrimer that enhances drought tolerance. This complex promotes stomatal closure, limits reactive oxygen species accumulation, and elevates abscisic acid levels. Mechanistically, the NF-Y trimer directly activates the drought-responsive genes SlAREB1 and SlDREB2 by binding the CCAAT motif, with SlNF-YA3a mediating DNA contact and the intact complex conferring maximal transcriptional activation. Notably, this activity is antagonized by SlWRKY16, which physically interacts with SlNF-YC9 and suppresses NF-Y-dependent transcription. Genetic analyses further support the cooperative function of SlNF-YC9 and SlNF-YB3b, as well as the antagonistic role of SlWRKY16, in regulating drought tolerance. Together, our findings define the NF-Y complex as a key regulatory component that coordinates positive and negative transcriptional inputs during the tomato drought response, providing a molecular framework for targeted crop improvement.

works.title: The point of disconnection: early-drought fine root shrinkage is driven by plant water use in Pinus radiata
works.abstract: Understanding the root-soil interface is essential for determining when plants become hydraulically isolated from their soil environment during drought. Emerging evidence suggests roots shrink substantially during dehydration, but the drivers and water-flow implications remain elusive, with few data linking shrinkage across soil and plant water status. Using Pinus radiata, a widespread isohydric conifer, we use synchrotron-based Micro-CT to scan intact roots < 2.5 mm in soil during mild plant drying (prior to embolism) to isolate relationships between shrinkage, soil (Ψsoil) and xylem (Ψplant) water potential. Fine roots in situ began shrinking during the earliest stages of Ψplant drying (-0.2 MPa to -0.88 MPa), losing 14.8 ± 10.3% initial transverse-sectional area (62% of observed shrinkage) prior to incipient soil drying (0-72 kPa Ψsoil). Ψplant was a significantly better predictor of shrinkage than Ψsoil, showing a linear shrinkage-Ψplant relationship across this early drying gradient when normalised to shrinkage at -1 MPa, accounting for variable initial Ψplant. Ψplant decline was linearly coordinated with cortical lacunae formation. This Ψplant-driven pattern identifies root shrinkage as an essential component of plant hydraulic function during commonly experienced water potential gradients, occurring long prior to stomatal closure and xylem embolism. This reveals water use from cortical tissues as a key physiological process defining plant-soil disconnection during water deficit.

works.title: Knocking-out the brassinosteroid biosynthesis genes DWARF1 or DWARF4 produces upright canopy architecture in wheat
works.abstract: Abstract Key message The wheat dwf4 brassinosteroid biosynthesis mutation confers an erect canopy architecture without yield penalties, unlike dwf1 , and is a promising target to develop ideotypes suitable for high-density planting. Abstract Brassinosteroids (BR) regulate multiple agronomic traits in plants, including leaf angle. BR depletion promotes an upright canopy architecture, which can improve vertical light distribution and grain yields in cereals under high planting densities. However, broad reductions in BR activity often negatively impact fertility and grain size. Spatially restricted modification of BR metabolism through targeting specific genes could, therefore, provide an erect canopy while minimising negative pleiotropic effects. In the BR biosynthesis pathway, DWARF1/DIMINUTO ( DWF1/DIM ) encodes a C-24 reductase that catalyses the production of the first committed sterol BR precursor, while DWF4 and DWF11 encode 22α-hydroxylase enzymes that act later in the pathway and exhibit partial functional redundancy. Using ethyl-methanesulphonate (EMS)-induced mutations that introduce premature stop codons, we generated wheat lines lacking functional copies of all three homoeologues of DWF1 and DWF4 in the Cadenza background. The dwf4-abd mutant displayed upright leaves and a slight height reduction but showed no differences in grain size or weight when tested in glasshouse and field conditions. The dwf1-abd mutant also produced an upright canopy, but tiller number, grain size and grain weight were reduced compared to the wild-type. The dwf1-abd mutant was hypersensitive to exogenous BR application. Metabolite profiling showed that concentrations of the BR precursors campesterol (CR), campestanol (CN) and 6-oxocampestanol (6-oxoCN) were significantly reduced in dwf1-abd seedlings compared to wild-type controls, whereas precursor levels were not reduced in dwf4-abd seedlings, consistent with gene redundancy.

works.title: TaqW-6BL, a novel gene positively regulates grain WE-AX content in wheat
ZmHY5L synergistically affects endosperm starch quality and grain morphology through G-box-mediated transcriptional regulation of the maize waxy gene
Exogenous riboflavin activates stress-responsive gene networks in Arabidopsis
works.abstract: Abstract Riboflavin is the precursor of the flavin mononucleotide (FMN) and flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) which are vital coenzymes to a wide array of plant metabolic processes. While the exogenous application of riboflavin has been well-documented to enhance plant stress tolerance, the molecular mechanisms underlying this protective effect remain largely unknown. Here, we present a comprehensive transcriptomic analysis of riboflavin-treated Arabidopsis seedlings, revealing significant changes in gene expression related to stress responses, signaling transduction and secondary metabolism. Riboflavin treatment altered the expression of genes within specific cellular functional categories, supporting the role of riboflavin in regulating plant metabolism and enhancing stress adaptation. The transcriptional changes indicate a shift from growth to stress management, potentially downregulating photosynthesis to preserve energy for immediate stress responses and protect against damage from excess light or oxidative stress. Further, we identified a feedback mechanism where elevated riboflavin levels regulate the expression of genes of its own biosynthetic pathway, controlling both its synthesis and chemical conversion processes. Our study provides novel and valuable insights into the gene expression mechanisms underlying riboflavin-mediated stress tolerance and highlights a potential application of exogenous riboflavin as a strategy for improving crop plasticity and adaptation in the face of environmental challenges.

works.title: Single-nucleus and spatial transcriptomics reveal dynamic cell differentiation and storage product accumulation in rice endosperm
works.abstract: Rice (Oryza sativa) endosperm, a major food source worldwide, accumulates starch, proteins, and lipids. Understanding the cellular and molecular mechanisms that govern endosperm development and storage product accumulation is crucial for improving grain yield and quality. Through single-nucleus and spatial transcriptomic analyses of 177,820 nuclei and 60,003 spatial spots across four developmental stages of the rice caryopsis, we identified 12 distinct cell types and delineated seven precise anatomical regions, thereby establishing a spatially resolved single-cell transcriptomic atlas of the developing rice endosperm. Using these cell type annotations, we inferred the developmental trajectories of endosperm cells, uncovered gene regulatory networks underlying cell differentiation, and identified three key transcription factors that regulate aleurone cell-fate determination. Furthermore, we observed cellular heterogeneity in the aleurone layer and the starchy endosperm and showed how this heterogeneity coordinates nutrient transport and storage product biosynthesis during rice grain filling. This study establishes a comprehensive cellular foundation and genetic regulatory network for understanding rice endosperm formation and storage product accumulation.

works.title: Chromosome-level phylogenomics and genome evolution of the grape family
ATM2 promotes phosphoinositide formation to stabilize actin–plasma membrane contacts in pollen tubes
Metabolically robust ratiometric autoluminescent reporters
works.abstract: Self-sustained luminescence enables non-invasive monitoring of molecular events at the whole-organism level, but its intensity depends on both gene expression and cellular metabolism, limiting quantitative interpretation. Here we present an approach that disentangles the contributions of gene expression and metabolism. By co-expressing an engineered reference luciferase variant that uses the same substrate but emits light at a different wavelength and monitoring the colour ratio, we substantially reduced signal variability, enabling quantitative physiological imaging despite changes in metabolic activity.

works.title: Rewriting wheat karyotypes through centromere-targeted chromosome engineering
Progress and perspectives in nitrogenase engineering in plants and yeast
works.abstract: Crop productivity relies on synthetic nitrogen fertilizers, which entail significant economic and environmental costs. Engineering crop plants to produce nitrogenase allowing them to acquire nitrogen from the atmosphere offers a transformative approach to sustainable agriculture. However, engineering the nitrogenase pathway into eukaryotic cells poses significant challenges due to the enzyme metal clusters, high energy demands, and extreme sensitivity to oxygen. This review summarizes recent advances in nitrogenase engineering in yeast and plants. Progress has been made using a stepwise modular approach and a functional validation pipeline for core and ancillary nitrogenase proteins. Key milestones include recovery of NifH with in vitro activity from mitochondria and chloroplasts, production of NifB that is active upon isolation or after in vitro cluster reconstitution, production of NifB-co in yeast mitochondria, in vitro FeMo-co biosynthesis using proteins purified from yeast mitochondria, and recovery of nitrogenase components from transgenic rice with activity demonstrated in vitro. Complete nitrogenase activity in engineered yeast or plants has not yet been demonstrated. We discuss the importance of organelle targeting, the exploitation of natural diversity and engineered proteins, and synthetic biology tools for the assembly of multigene pathways. Finally, we present the main remaining obstacles, such as the assembly of functional NifDK in plants, integration with host metabolism and coordinated regulation, and we outline the prospects for the development of nitrogen-fixing crops.

works.title: Plant Nutrient Homeostasis In A Rising CO2 World
works.abstract: The rapid rise in atmospheric CO2 concentration presents a critical paradox for global agriculture: while it stimulates photosynthesis and plant productivity, it simultaneously compromises crop nutritional quality. This decline in quality is linked to a lower concentration of essential macro- and micronutrients in crop edible parts, involving complex regulatory shifts that go beyond the simple growth dilution effect caused by the decoupling between growth and nutrient uptake. In this review, we summarize the current knowledge regarding the impact of elevated CO2 (eCO2) on nitrogen (N) nutrition, among other aspects, discussing how the availability of nitrate (NO3-) or ammonium (NH4+) affects plant growth and N status under eCO2, a long-standing debate in the field. We outline recent advances in the signalling mechanisms regulating NO3- uptake under eCO2 and discuss the interaction between photorespiration and the assimilation of both N sources. Likewise, we address the main effects and regulatory mechanisms associated with eCO2 and the homeostasis of sulphur (S), phosphorus (P) and the micronutrients iron (Fe) and zinc (Zn). Collectively, we intend to provide a comprehensive framework to guide future crop breeding and climate-resilient agronomic management.

works.title: Understanding Leaf Surface‐Specific Stomatal Traits and Their Effects on Barley Grain Yield
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Spring barley yields are highly variable, depending mostly on early season precipitation and temperature. Stomatal traits (stomatal conductance, size, density, adaxial to abaxial stomatal density ratio and conductance ratio) are important determinants of plant production and stress tolerance. Here, we determined stomatal traits of penultimate and flag leaves and grain yields of thirteen barley genotypes during a 3‐year field experiment in Estonia. We found that adaxial to abaxial stomatal density ratio was mostly determined by environment in penultimate leaves. Grain yields ranged from 2400 to 6100 kg ha −1 in our study. Correlations between stomatal traits and grain yield were found in the pooled dataset due to strong effects of annual abiotic conditions on studied traits. Penultimate leaf ratios of adaxial to abaxial stomatal density and conductance correlated positively with grain yield in the pooled dataset. In 2022 and 2023, the stomatal conductance ratio also correlated with grain yield, however, no other stomatal trait correlated with grain yield in any individual year, although stomatal traits differed significantly between genotypes.
